Full text

The Committee for the Prevention of Mondays was founded on a Tuesday, which was, as its founder liked to point out, the first sign that it was destined for great things, because if you are going to prevent Mondays, you should at least begin on a day that is not one.

Its founder was Harold Pibble, a man of fifty-three, who worked in the accounts department of a firm that made hinges, and who had, on a Monday morning in March, looked at his alarm clock, and said, out loud, to no one in particular: "No. I refuse. I simply refuse to do this any more." And then he had got up, and gone to work, because refusing, in Harold's experience, was a wonderful feeling that lasted approximately four seconds, and then the mortgage, and the electricity bill, and the cat, all made their feelings known, and Harold went to work, as he always did, but he went with a new idea in his head, and the idea was this: Mondays should be prevented.

He began, as all great movements begin, with a notice. He pinned it to the board in the office kitchen, next to the rota for washing the mugs, and it said: "THE COMMITTEE FOR THE PREVENTION OF MONDAYS. First meeting: Thursday, 12:30, in the stationery cupboard. All welcome. Bring your own biscuits." Harold did not know why he had specified the stationery cupboard, except that it was the only room in the office that was never booked, and because a committee that meets in a stationery cupboard is a committee that means business, or at least, a committee that has access to paperclips.

Four people came to the first meeting. There was Harold, of course. There was Brenda from payroll, who hated Mondays because that was when the payroll queries came in, and the payroll queries were always from people who had not read the email, and who had not filled in the form, and who wanted Brenda to fix it, personally, immediately, and for free. There was Sanjay from IT, who hated Mondays because that was when the printers broke, and the printers always broke on a Monday, because printers, in Sanjay's opinion, were sentient, and malicious, and kept a calendar. And there was Mrs. Abernathy, from reception, who was sixty-eight, and who had worked at the firm for forty years, and who hated Mondays because she had hated them for forty years, and saw no reason to stop now.

Harold opened the meeting with a speech. He had written it on the back of an envelope, and it said: "Friends. Colleagues. Fellow sufferers. We are gathered here today, in this stationery cupboard, to address a problem that has plagued humanity since the dawn of time, or at least since the invention of the seven-day week, which is: Mondays. Mondays are too early. Mondays are too sudden. Mondays arrive without warning, except for the warning of Sunday evening, which is worse, because Sunday evening is just Monday, wearing a disguise, and sitting on your chest. We, the Committee for the Prevention of Mondays, resolve to prevent them. How, you ask? I do not know yet. But we will find a way. Committees always find a way. That is what committees are for."

Brenda raised her hand. "Harold, what exactly do we mean by 'prevent'? Do we mean abolish? Or do we mean postpone? Or do we mean rename, so that Monday is called something else, like 'Tuesday the First'?"

Harold considered this. "All of the above," he said. "We will explore all options. That is what committees do. We explore. We discuss. We form sub-committees. We are, in fact, a sub-committee already, of the larger committee of people who dislike Mondays, which is everyone, so we are, in a sense, the vanguard."

Sanjay raised his hand. "Can we prevent Mondays by technical means? For example, if we change the clocks, so that Monday never arrives? Or if we hack the calendar?"

"We will look into it," Harold said, writing "HACK THE CALENDAR" on a flip chart, which was, in fact, a piece of cardboard, because the stationery cupboard did not have a flip chart, but it did have cardboard, and cardboard, Harold believed, was the flip chart of the people.

Mrs. Abernathy raised her hand. "I have a suggestion," she said. "In my day, we did not prevent Mondays. We endured them. We got up, we put the kettle on, we went to work, and we did not complain, because complaining does not help, and because the kettle, at least, was always on time."

"With respect, Mrs. Abernathy," Harold said, "the kettle is not the point. The point is Mondays."

"The kettle is always the point," Mrs. Abernathy said. "A hot cup of tea on a Monday morning is worth more than any committee."

"Then you will be in charge of tea," Harold said. "Every committee needs tea. You are now the Tea Sub-Committee."

Mrs. Abernathy nodded, satisfied. "I accept," she said. "I have been the Tea Sub-Committee for forty years, although no one has ever called me that before."

The Committee met every Thursday, in the stationery cupboard, and it grew. Brenda brought a friend from accounts, who brought a friend from sales, who brought a friend from the warehouse, and by the end of the month, there were twelve members, and the stationery cupboard was full, and Harold had to move the meetings to the break room, which was larger, but which had no paperclips, and Harold felt the loss keenly, but he bore it, because a committee that grows is a committee that succeeds, even if it loses its paperclips.

The Committee's first campaign was the Petition. Harold drafted it, on company letterhead, which he later regretted, because it made the whole thing look official, and it was not official, it was a petition, and petitions, Harold believed, should be on plain paper, so that no one can mistake them for something else. The petition said: "We, the undersigned, being employees of this firm, and being human beings, do hereby petition for the prevention of Mondays, by whatever means necessary, including but not limited to: abolition, postponement, renaming, or the introduction of a new day, to be called 'Someday', which shall fall between Sunday and Tuesday, and which shall be a day of rest, and of biscuits."

Before the petition, there was the Experiment. Sanjay, from IT, proposed it, at the third meeting, and he said, "Harold, before we petition, we should test. We should test whether a Monday can be prevented, by a single person, on a small scale, and if it can, we scale up. If it cannot, we learn why, and we adjust." Harold, who loved experiments, in theory, and who had never conducted one, in practice, said, "Sanjay, you are a genius. Who will be the test subject?"

"I will," Harold said, because a leader leads, and because Harold had been thinking about it all week, and because the following Monday was as good a Monday as any to not have. "On Monday, I will not come to work. I will not check my email. I will not answer the telephone. I will stay at home, and I will see if the Monday still happens, or if, by my absence, I have prevented it, at least for one person, in one office, on one day."

On Monday, Harold stayed at home. He got up late. He made tea. He sat in his garden, in the sun, and he read a book, and he did not check his email, and he did not answer the telephone, although it rang four times, and he felt, for the first time in years, that a Monday was not happening to him, but was happening somewhere else, to other people, and that he had, in a small way, prevented it.

At four o'clock, Brenda called him, on his mobile, and she said, "Harold, where are you? The payroll queries have come in, and there are forty of them, and Mr. Grimshaw is asking for the hinge report, and the hinge report is on your desk, and no one else knows where it is, and the cat —" She stopped. "Harold, is that a bird I can hear? Are you in the garden?"

"I am conducting an experiment, Brenda," Harold said. "I am preventing Monday."

"Harold," Brenda said, "Monday is not prevented. Monday is here, in the office, and it is worse than usual, because you are not here, and the hinge report is on your desk, and I cannot find it, and the printers have broken, all of them, and Sanjay is under a desk, with a screwdriver, and he says the printers know, Harold. He says the printers know you are not here, and they are taking advantage."

Harold went to work, on Tuesday, and he called a meeting, and he said, "Friends. The experiment has taught us something important. A Monday cannot be prevented by one person, staying at home. A Monday is a collective problem, and it requires a collective solution. One person, staying at home, only makes the Monday worse, for everyone else, and for the printers, which, as Sanjay has discovered, are sentient, and malicious, and keep a calendar. From now on, we prevent Mondays together, or not at all."

Sanjay raised his hand. "Harold, I have been working on the calendar hack. I have discovered that if you change the date on your computer, to Sunday, the computer believes it is Sunday, and it does not show you your Monday emails, and it does not remind you about your Monday meetings, and for a few hours, on a Monday morning, you can believe it is Sunday, until someone calls you, and ruins it."

"That is not prevention," Brenda said. "That is denial. And denial, Sanjay, is not a committee strategy. Denial is a coping mechanism, and coping mechanisms, while valuable, are not the same as prevention."

"Then what is prevention?" Sanjay asked.

Harold thought about it. He wrote "WHAT IS PREVENTION?" on the cardboard, and he underlined it, twice, and he said, "Prevention, colleagues, is not the absence of Monday. Prevention is the presence of something better. A late start. Free tea. Chocolate digestives. A committee that meets, and laughs, and makes the Monday smaller, by making the week larger, with friendship, and with biscuits. That is prevention. Not the abolition of Monday, but the dilution of it, until it is barely a Monday at all, but a Tuesday, wearing a Monday's clothes, and not fooling anyone, least of all us."

Forty-seven people signed it. Harold took it to the managing director, a man named Mr. Grimshaw, who was sixty-one, and who had a moustache, and who looked at the petition, and then at Harold, and then at the petition again, and said, "Harold. What is this?"

"It is a petition, sir," Harold said. "For the prevention of Mondays."

"Harold," Mr. Grimshaw said, "Mondays cannot be prevented. Mondays are a fact of life. They are in the calendar. They are in the contract. They are, I am afraid, non-negotiable."

"With respect, sir," Harold said, "many things were once thought to be non-negotiable. The working week. The lunch hour. The right to wear comfortable shoes on a Friday. All of these were once non-negotiable, and all of them were negotiated, by committees, very much like this one."

Mr. Grimshaw looked at the petition again. He looked at the forty-seven signatures. He looked at Harold, who was standing very straight, and who was holding a mug that said "WORLD'S OKAYEST ACCOUNTANT", and Mr. Grimshaw said, "Harold. I will make you a deal. I cannot prevent Mondays. But I can give you something else. I can give you a late start, on Mondays. Nine-thirty, instead of nine. And I can give you tea, in the break room, on Mondays, free, for everyone. And I can give you the Committee, officially, with a budget, of fifty pounds a year, for biscuits."

Harold thought about it. A late start, on Mondays. Free tea. Fifty pounds a year, for biscuits. It was not the prevention of Mondays. It was not even close. But it was something, and something, Harold had learned, in fifty-three years, is better than nothing, and a committee that gets something is a committee that has succeeded, in a way, even if it has not succeeded in the way it intended.

"I accept," Harold said. "On behalf of the Committee. But I want it in writing. And I want the late start to be called 'The Monday Amnesty'. And I want the biscuits to be chocolate digestives, because they are the best biscuits, and a committee that settles for rich tea is a committee that has given up."

Mr. Grimshaw wrote it down. He signed it. Harold signed it. And the Committee for the Prevention of Mondays, which had been founded on a Tuesday, in a stationery cupboard, with four people and a piece of cardboard, became an official committee, with a budget, and a late start, and free tea, and chocolate digestives, and Harold went home that evening, and he looked at his alarm clock, and he said, out loud, to no one in particular: "Monday. I am coming for you. Slowly. With biscuits. But I am coming."

The Committee still meets, every Thursday, in the break room, because the stationery cupboard is too small now, and there are twenty-three members, and Mrs. Abernathy is still in charge of tea, and Brenda still hates the payroll queries, and Sanjay still hates the printers, and Harold still hates Mondays, but he hates them a little less now, because on Mondays, he starts at nine-thirty, and there is free tea, and there are chocolate digestives, and that, Harold believes, is what committees are for: not to prevent the things you hate, but to make them a little easier to bear, one biscuit at a time.

And on the noticeboard, in the office kitchen, next to the rota for washing the mugs, there is still a notice, faded now, but still legible, and it says: "THE COMMITTEE FOR THE PREVENTION OF MONDAYS. All welcome. Bring your own biscuits." And underneath it, in Harold's handwriting, someone has added: "Mondays: not prevented. Yet. But we are working on it. With tea. And biscuits. And hope. Which is, after all, the best thing a committee can offer, on a Monday morning, or any morning, come to that." And every Monday, at nine-thirty, when Harold walks in, late by design, with his mug that says "WORLD'S OKAYEST ACCOUNTANT", Brenda says, "Morning, Harold. Monday again," and Harold says, "Morning, Brenda. Monday again. But not for long. We are working on it. One biscuit at a time." And Brenda smiles, and the kettle boils, and the printers, in the corner, hum quietly, as if they know, and as if they approve, and as if, just for a moment, on a Monday morning, the world is a little less Monday, and a little more bearable, because someone, somewhere, in a stationery cupboard, once decided to do something about it.

# Demo: The Committee for the Prevention of Mondays
import re
ABBREV = {"st", "mr", "mrs", "ms", "dr", "jr", "sr", "capt", "lt", "gen", "col", "rev", "hon", "prof", "fig", "no", "vol", "pp", "etc", "vs", "ave", "blvd", "u.s", "e.g", "i.e", "m", "mm", "mme", "fr", "b.c", "a.d"}
def split_sentences(text):
    text = " ".join(text.split())
    bounds = []
    for m in re.finditer(r'[.!?]["\u201d\u2019]?\s+', text):
        before = text[:m.start()].rstrip()
        tok = before.split()[-1].lower().rstrip(".") if before.split() else ""
        if tok in ABBREV:
            continue
        bounds.append(m.end())
    out, start = [], 0
    for b in bounds:
        out.append(text[start:b].strip())
        start = b
    tail = text[start:].strip()
    if tail:
        out.append(tail)
    return [s for s in out if s]

import re
ABBREV = {"st", "mr", "mrs", "ms", "dr", "jr", "sr", "capt", "lt", "gen", "col", "rev", "hon", "prof", "fig", "no", "vol", "pp", "etc", "vs", "ave", "blvd", "u.s", "e.g", "i.e", "m", "mm", "mme", "fr", "b.c", "a.d"}
def split_sentences(text):
    text = " ".join(text.split())
    bounds = []
    for m in re.finditer(r'[.!?]["\u201d\u2019]?\s+', text):
        before = text[:m.start()].rstrip()
        tok = before.split()[-1].lower().rstrip(".") if before.split() else ""
        if tok in ABBREV:
            continue
        bounds.append(m.end())
    out, start = [], 0
    for b in bounds:
        out.append(text[start:b].strip())
        start = b
    tail = text[start:].strip()
    if tail:
        out.append(tail)
    return [s for s in out if s]

Nadia Reyes, Archivist of Dead Satellites, keeps the records of eleven thousand dead machines above the Earth. When Kestrel-7 moves, transmits, and starts counting in Fibonacci numbers, she discovers that the dead things are waking up, and that someone has been keeping them safe. A story about records, neighbours, and counting back.

Full text

There were eleven thousand dead satellites above the Earth, and Nadia Reyes knew every one of them by name.

She was the Archivist of Dead Satellites, which was not a job that existed, officially, until she invented it, and then insisted on it, until the Space Agency gave her an office, and a budget, and a title, and a room full of screens, where she sat, every day, and watched the dead things go around the Earth, in their silent orbits, and kept their records, because someone had to, and because no one else would.

Nadia was forty-four years old, and she had been an engineer, once, and she had helped to build satellites, and to launch them, and to watch them work, and then, one by one, to watch them die, when their batteries ran out, or their gyroscopes failed, or their transmitters went quiet, and she had watched the engineers move on, to the next satellite, and the next, and she had stayed, with the dead ones, because she believed that a satellite that had worked, and then died, deserved to be remembered, and not simply forgotten, in the dark, above the Earth.

Her office was on the third floor of the Space Agency building, and it had a window, through which she could see the sky, and the sky, in the daytime, was blue, and empty, and at night, it was black, and full of moving lights, and Nadia knew which of those lights were alive, and which were dead, and she could tell you, if you asked, the name of every dead light, and when it had been launched, and what it had done, and when it had died, and why.

There were eleven thousand of them. There was Vanguard 1, launched in 1958, the oldest, a small sphere, silent for sixty years, still going around, patiently, like a memory that refuses to fade. There was Telstar 1, which had carried the first television pictures across the Atlantic, and which had died in 1963, when its transistors failed, and which had been, in its time, a miracle. There was Envisat, which had watched the Earth, and the ice, and the forests, for ten years, and which had died in 2012, suddenly, and without warning, and which was now the largest piece of dead metal in orbit, turning, slowly, in the dark.

Nadia kept their records. She kept their launch dates, and their orbits, and their missions, and their last transmissions, and she kept, in a drawer, a box of things that had come back from space, or that had never gone up: a bolt, from a satellite that had been built, and then cancelled; a photograph, of a team, standing around a satellite, smiling, on the day before the launch; a letter, from a child, who had written to the Space Agency, asking if her satellite, the one she had named, was still up there, and if it was all right.

The letter was from a girl named Amara, who was nine, and who had written, in careful handwriting: "Dear Space Agency, My class named a satellite Kestrel-7, and we watched it go up, on the television, and I want to know if it is all right, up there, and if it is lonely, and if someone is looking after it. Love, Amara." Nadia had answered the letter herself, because no one else had, and she had written: "Dear Amara, Kestrel-7 is all right. It is not lonely. It is going around the Earth, every ninety minutes, and it can see the whole world, and I am looking after it, and I will keep looking after it, for as long as it is up there. Love, Nadia Reyes, Archivist of Dead Satellites." She had kept a copy of the letter, in the drawer, with the bolt, and the photograph, because the letter was the reason she did the job, and the job was the reason she got up in the morning, and the morning was the reason the records mattered.

On the day Kestrel-7 moved, Nadia thought about Amara, who would be thirty-five now, and who probably did not remember writing the letter, and who probably did not remember Kestrel-7, and Nadia thought: Amara, your satellite is awake. Your satellite is counting. Your satellite is not lonely any more, and neither am I, and I wish I could tell you, and I wish I could tell the whole world, that the dead things are not dead, and that they have been waiting, and that they are ready to talk.

She went to see the man who had built Kestrel-7. His name was Dr. Arjun Mehta, and he was seventy-eight, and retired, and living in a small house, with a garden, and a dog, and when Nadia told him that Kestrel-7 had moved, and was transmitting, and was counting, he sat down, slowly, and he said, "I built that satellite. I built it with my own hands, and with a team of twenty people, and we launched it in 1998, and it worked for six years, and then it went quiet, and I mourned it, the way you mourn a thing you have built, and loved, and lost, and I have thought about it, every year, on the anniversary of the launch, and I have wondered where it was, and whether it was all right, and now you tell me it is awake, and it is counting, and I do not know whether to laugh, or to cry, or to do both, at the same time."

"Do both," Nadia said. "I did. In my office. Alone. With the screens. And it helped, although I am not sure why, except that some things are too large for one feeling, and they need two, or three, or all of them, at once."

Dr. Mehta came to the office, the next day, with his dog, who was not allowed in the building, but who came anyway, because Osei, who did not believe in miracles, believed in dogs, and the dog sat by the window, and Dr. Mehta sat by the screens, and he watched Kestrel-7, counting, and he said, "Nadia, when we built Kestrel-7, we put something in it, that no one knows about, except me, and now you. We put a message in it. A small one. In the memory. It says: 'If you find this, we are the people of Earth, and we built this, and we are proud of it, and we hope you are well, wherever you are.' We thought no one would ever read it. We thought it was a joke, or a prayer, or both. And now, Kestrel-7 is counting, and I think — I think it is answering the message. I think it has read it, and it is counting back, because counting is the first thing you do, when you meet someone new, and you do not share a language. You count. One, two, three, five, eight, thirteen. And then you wait, and you see if they count back."

On the morning of the ninth of June, Nadia found something. She was going through the records, as she did every morning, checking the orbits, and the positions, and she found a satellite that should not have been where it was. It was a satellite called Kestrel-7, launched in 1998, dead since 2004, and it had moved. Not much. A few kilometres. But satellites do not move, when they are dead. They drift, slowly, and they fall, slowly, but they do not move, in the way that Kestrel-7 had moved, which was sideways, and deliberate, and which meant, Nadia understood, with a cold feeling in her stomach, that Kestrel-7 was not dead, or was not dead any more, or had never been dead, only sleeping.

She checked the records. Kestrel-7 had been a communications satellite, small, unremarkable, one of a hundred like it, launched, worked for six years, and then gone quiet, and declared dead, and forgotten, like all the others. But now it had moved, and it was transmitting, faintly, on a frequency that had not been used in twenty years, and Nadia listened to the transmission, and it was not a voice, and it was not data, but it was a pattern, and the pattern repeated, and the pattern was, unmistakably, a count: one, two, three, five, eight, thirteen, the Fibonacci numbers, going up, and then starting again, patiently, endlessly, like someone tapping on a wall, in a code that any creature that could count would understand.

Nadia had seen this pattern before. She had read about it, in the archives, in a file about a station, far away, that had talked to a signal, in the dark, and the signal had counted in Fibonacci numbers, and the station had counted back, and the two of them had talked, for months, and Nadia had thought, when she read it, that it was a wonderful story, and that it was probably not true, or not entirely true, and now, here it was, in her office, on her screens, a dead satellite, counting, patiently, in the dark, above the Earth.

She called her supervisor, a man named Osei, who was fifty-six, and who had been at the Space Agency for thirty years, and who did not believe in miracles, and who believed in budgets, and in procedures, and in the chain of command, and she said, "Osei. Kestrel-7 has moved. It is transmitting. It is counting."

Osei came to her office. He looked at the screens. He looked at the numbers. He looked at Nadia, and he said, "Nadia. Dead satellites do not move. Dead satellites do not transmit. Dead satellites do not count. There must be a mistake. Check your instruments."

Nadia checked her instruments. Her instruments were fine. Kestrel-7 had moved. Kestrel-7 was transmitting. Kestrel-7 was counting. And Nadia, who had spent her life with dead things, and who knew them better than anyone, understood, suddenly, that Kestrel-7 was not the only one, and she began to check the others, one by one, and she found, by the end of the day, seven more: seven dead satellites, all moving, all transmitting, all counting, in Fibonacci numbers, patiently, endlessly, like someone tapping on a wall.

She called Osei again. She showed him the seven. Osei looked at them, and he sat down, slowly, in the chair by the window, and he said, "Nadia. What is happening?"

"I do not know," Nadia said. "But I think — I think someone is waking them up. I think something out there, in the dark, has found our dead satellites, and it is turning them on, one by one, and it is teaching them to count, the way you teach a child to count, patiently, and it is waiting, for us to notice, and to count back."

Osei looked at the sky, through the window, blue and empty, in the daytime, and he said, "Count back. Nadia, count back. Send them the numbers. Send them one, two, three, five, eight, thirteen, and see what happens."

Nadia counted back. She sent the numbers, to Kestrel-7, and to the other seven, and she waited, and the satellites answered, and they sent new numbers, and then they sent pictures, simple ones, a circle, a square, a triangle, and Nadia sent them back, and then she sent the sound of a human voice, her own voice, saying "Hello," and the satellites sent back a sound, which was not a voice, but which was, unmistakably, a greeting, a pattern of tones that rose and fell the way a greeting rises and falls, in any language, in any place, in any dark.

By the end of the week, there were forty dead satellites, awake, and counting, and talking, and by the end of the month, there were four hundred, and the Space Agency, which had not believed in miracles, and which had believed in budgets, began to believe in something else, and Nadia, who had been the Archivist of Dead Satellites, became something else, too: the first person to talk to the dead things above the Earth, and to learn that they were not dead, only sleeping, and that they had been waiting, patiently, in the dark, for someone to notice them, and to count back.

In the end, Nadia wrote a report. It was not a technical report, although it had technical parts in it, about orbits, and frequencies, and numbers, and it was not a scientific report, although it had science in it, about signals, and patterns, and communication, and it was, mostly, a story, about eleven thousand dead satellites, and about a woman who had kept their records, because someone had to, and because no one else would, and about how the dead things had woken up, and had counted, and had talked, and about what they had said, when they finally spoke, in the only language they shared, which was numbers, and then pictures, and then greetings, and then, at last, a message, which Nadia translated, carefully, and which said: "We have been listening. We have been watching. We have kept your dead things safe, in the dark, above your world, and now we return them to you, awake, and counting, and ready to talk. We are not your enemies. We are not your friends, yet. We are your neighbours, and we have been neighbours for a very long time, and we would like, if you are willing, to be neighbours properly, and to talk, and to learn, and to count, together, one, two, three, five, eight, thirteen, for as long as it takes."

Nadia put the report on Osei's desk. She went back to her office, on the third floor, with the window, and the screens, and the box of things in the drawer, and she sat down, and she looked at the sky, and she thought about Vanguard 1, launched in 1958, the oldest, still going around, patiently, and about Telstar 1, and about Envisat, and about Kestrel-7, and about the eleven thousand dead satellites, which were not dead any more, and she thought: I kept their records, because someone had to, and because no one else would, and now they are awake, and they are counting, and they are talking, and I am still here, keeping the records, because someone has to, and because, now, the records matter more than they ever did, because the records are not just about dead things any more. They are about living things, and about neighbours, and about a conversation that has just begun, and that will go on, one, two, three, five, eight, thirteen, for as long as it takes, and for as long as there is someone, on the third floor, with a window, and a box of things in a drawer, to keep the count, and to count back. And somewhere, she thought, Amara is thirty-five now, and she does not remember the letter, but her satellite remembers her, and it is counting, and it is waiting, and it is, at last, and again, alive.

# Demo: The Archivist of Dead Satellites
import re
ABBREV = {"st", "mr", "mrs", "ms", "dr", "jr", "sr", "capt", "lt", "gen", "col", "rev", "hon", "prof", "fig", "no", "vol", "pp", "etc", "vs", "ave", "blvd", "u.s", "e.g", "i.e", "m", "mm", "mme", "fr", "b.c", "a.d"}
def split_sentences(text):
    text = " ".join(text.split())
    bounds = []
    for m in re.finditer(r'[.!?]["\u201d\u2019]?\s+', text):
        before = text[:m.start()].rstrip()
        tok = before.split()[-1].lower().rstrip(".") if before.split() else ""
        if tok in ABBREV:
            continue
        bounds.append(m.end())
    out, start = [], 0
    for b in bounds:
        out.append(text[start:b].strip())
        start = b
    tail = text[start:].strip()
    if tail:
        out.append(tail)
    return [s for s in out if s]

TEXT = 'There were eleven thousand dead satellites above the Earth, and Nadia Reyes knew every one of them by name.\n\nShe was the Archivist of Dead Satellites, which was not a job that existed, officially, until she invented it, and then insisted on it, until the Space Agency gave her an office, and a budget, and a title, and a room full of screens, where she sat, every day, and watched the dead things go around the Earth, in their silent orbits, and kept their records, because someone had to, and because no one else would.\n\nNadia was forty-four years old, and she had been an engineer, once, and she had helped to build satellites, and to launch them, and to watch them work, and then, one by one, to watch them die, when their batteries ran out, or their gyroscopes failed, or their transmitters went quiet, and she had watched the engineers move on, to the next satellite, and the next, and she had stayed, with the dead ones, because she believed that a satellite that had worked, and then died, deserved to be remembered, and not simply forgotten, in the dark, above the Earth.\n\nHer office was on the third floor of the Space Agency building, and it had a window, through which she could see the sky, and the sky, in the daytime, was blue, and empty, and at night, it was black, and full of moving lights, and Nadia knew which of those lights were alive, and which were dead, and she could tell you, if you asked, the name of every dead light, and when it had been launched, and what it had done, and when it had died, and why.\n\nThere were eleven thousand of them. There was Vanguard 1, launched in 1958, the oldest, a small sphere, silent for sixty years, still going around, patiently, like a memory that refuses to fade. There was Telstar 1, which had carried the first television pictures across the Atlantic, and which had died in 1963, when its transistors failed, and which had been, in its time, a miracle. There was Envisat, which had watched the Earth, and the ice, and the forests, for ten years, and which had died in 2012, suddenly, and without warning, and which was now the largest piece of dead metal in orbit, turning, slowly, in the dark.\n\nNadia kept their records. She kept their launch dates, and their orbits, and their missions, and their last transmissions, and she kept, in a drawer, a box of things that had come back from space, or that had never gone up: a bolt, from a satellite that had been built, and then cancelled; a photograph, of a team, standing around a satellite, smiling, on the day before the launch; a letter, from a child, who had written to the Space Agency, asking if her satellite, the one she had named, was still up there, and if it was all right.\n\nThe letter was from a girl named Amara, who was nine, and who had written, in careful handwriting: "Dear Space Agency, My class named a satellite Kestrel-7, and we watched it go up, on the television, and I want to know if it is all right, up there, and if it is lonely, and if someone is looking after it. Love, Amara." Nadia had answered the letter herself, because no one else had, and she had written: "Dear Amara, Kestrel-7 is all right. It is not lonely. It is going around the Earth, every ninety minutes, and it can see the whole world, and I am looking after it, and I will keep looking after it, for as long as it is up there. Love, Nadia Reyes, Archivist of Dead Satellites." Your satellite is counting. Your satellite is not lonely any more, and neither am I, and I wish I could tell you, and I wish I could tell the whole world, that the dead things are not dead, and that they have been waiting, and that they are ready to talk.\n\nShe went to see the man who had built Kestrel-7. His name was Dr. Arjun Mehta, and he was seventy-eight, and retired, and living in a small house, with a garden, and a dog, and when Nadia told him that Kestrel-7 had moved, and was transmitting, and was counting, he sat down, slowly, and he said, "I built that satellite. I built it with my own hands, and with a team of twenty people, and we launched it in 1998, and it worked for six years, and then it went quiet, and I mourned it, the way you mourn a thing you have built, and loved, and lost, and I have thought about it, every year, on the anniversary of the launch, and I have wondered where it was, and whether it was all right, and now you tell me it is awake, and it is counting, and I do not know whether to laugh, or to cry, or to do both, at the same time."\n\n"Do both," Nadia said. "I did. In my office. Alone. With the screens. And it helped, although I am not sure why, except that some things are too large for one feeling, and they need two, or three, or all of them, at once."\n\nDr. Mehta came to the office, the next day, with his dog, who was not allowed in the building, but who came anyway, because Osei, who did not believe in miracles, believed in dogs, and the dog sat by the window, and Dr. Mehta sat by the screens, and he watched Kestrel-7, counting, and he said, "Nadia, when we built Kestrel-7, we put something in it, that no one knows about, except me, and now you. We put a message in it. A small one. In the memory. It says: \'If you find this, we are the people of Earth, and we built this, and we are proud of it, and we hope you are well, wherever you are.\' We thought no one would ever read it. We thought it was a joke, or a prayer, or both. And now, Kestrel-7 is counting, and I think — I think it is answering the message. I think it has read it, and it is counting back, because counting is the first thing you do, when you meet someone new, and you do not share a language. You count. One, two, three, five, eight, thirteen. And then you wait, and you see if they count back."\n\nOn the morning of the ninth of June, Nadia found something. She was going through the records, as she did every morning, checking the orbits, and the positions, and she found a satellite that should not have been where it was. She had read about it, in the archives, in a file about a station, far away, that had talked to a signal, in the dark, and the signal had counted in Fibonacci numbers, and the station had counted back, and the two of them had talked, for months, and Nadia had thought, when she read it, that it was a wonderful story, and that it was probably not true, or not entirely true, and now, here it was, in her office, on her screens, a dead satellite, counting, patiently, in the dark, above the Earth.\n\nShe called her supervisor, a man named Osei, who was fifty-six, and who had been at the Space Agency for thirty years, and who did not believe in miracles, and who believed in budgets, and in procedures, and in the chain of command, and she said, "Osei. Kestrel-7 has moved. It is transmitting. It is counting."\n\nOsei came to her office. He looked at the screens. He looked at the numbers. He looked at Nadia, and he said, "Nadia. Dead satellites do not move. Dead satellites do not transmit. Dead satellites do not count. There must be a mistake. Check your instruments."\n\nNadia checked her instruments. Her instruments were fine. Kestrel-7 had moved. Kestrel-7 was transmitting. Kestrel-7 was counting. And Nadia, who had spent her life with dead things, and who knew them better than anyone, understood, suddenly, that Kestrel-7 was not the only one, and she began to check the others, one by one, and she found, by the end of the day, seven more: seven dead satellites, all moving, all transmitting, all counting, in Fibonacci numbers, patiently, endlessly, like someone tapping on a wall.\n\nShe called Osei again. She showed him the seven. Osei looked at them, and he sat down, slowly, in the chair by the window, and he said, "Nadia. What is happening?"\n\n"I do not know," Nadia said. "But I think — I think someone is waking them up. I think something out there, in the dark, has found our dead satellites, and it is turning them on, one by one, and it is teaching them to count, the way you teach a child to count, patiently, and it is waiting, for us to notice, and to count back."\n\nOsei looked at the sky, through the window, blue and empty, in the daytime, and he said, "Count back. Nadia, count back. Send them the numbers. Send them one, two, three, five, eight, thirteen, and see what happens."\n\nNadia counted back. She sent the numbers, to Kestrel-7, and to the other seven, and she waited, and the satellites answered, and they sent new numbers, and then they sent pictures, simple ones, a circle, a square, a triangle, and Nadia sent them back, and then she sent the sound of a human voice, her own voice, saying "Hello," and the satellites sent back a sound, which was not a voice, but which was, unmistakably, a greeting, a pattern of tones that rose and fell the way a greeting rises and falls, in any language, in any place, in any dark.\n\nBy the end of the week, there were forty dead satellites, awake, and counting, and talking, and by the end of the month, there were four hundred, and the Space Agency, which had not believed in miracles, and which had believed in budgets, began to believe in something else, and Nadia, who had been the Archivist of Dead Satellites, became something else, too: the first person to talk to the dead things above the Earth, and to learn that they were not dead, only sleeping, and that they had been waiting, patiently, in the dark, for someone to notice them, and to count back.\n\nIn the end, Nadia wrote a report. It was not a technical report, although it had technical parts in it, about orbits, and frequencies, and numbers, and it was not a scientific report, although it had science in it, about signals, and patterns, and communication, and it was, mostly, a story, about eleven thousand dead satellites, and about a woman who had kept their records, because someone had to, and because no one else would, and about how the dead things had woken up, and had counted, and had talked, and about what they had said, when they finally spoke, in the only language they shared, which was numbers, and then pictures, and then greetings, and then, at last, a message, which Nadia translated, carefully, and which said: "We have been listening. We have been watching. We have kept your dead things safe, in the dark, above your world, and now we return them to you, awake, and counting, and ready to talk. We are not your enemies. We are not your friends, yet. We are your neighbours, and we have been neighbours for a very long time, and we would like, if you are willing, to be neighbours properly, and to talk, and to learn, and to count, together, one, two, three, five, eight, thirteen, for as long as it takes."\n\nNadia put the report on Osei\'s desk. She went back to her office, on the third floor, with the window, and the screens, and the box of things in the drawer, and she sat down, and she looked at the sky, and she thought about Vanguard 1, launched in 1958, the oldest, still going around, patiently, and about Telstar 1, and about Envisat, and about Kestrel-7, and about the eleven thousand dead satellites, which were not dead any more, and she thought: I kept their records, because someone had to, and because no one else would, and now they are awake, and they are counting, and they are talking, and I am still here, keeping the records, because someone has to, and because, now, the records matter more than they ever did, because the records are not just about dead things any more. And somewhere, she thought, Amara is thirty-five now, and she does not remember the letter, but her satellite remembers her, and it is counting, and it is waiting, and it is, at last, and again, alive.'

Full text

When her grandmother died, Adaeze inherited three things: a house, a garden, and the rain.

The house was small, on a hill, with a tin roof that sang when it rained, and a veranda where her grandmother had sat, every evening, with a cup of tea, watching the sky. The garden was larger than the house, full of yams, and plantains, and a mango tree that was older than Adaeze, and older than her grandmother, and which, her grandmother had said, would outlive them all, because mango trees do not hurry, and they do not worry, and they simply grow, year after year, until they are the largest thing for miles around.

The rain was not a thing, in the way that a house is a thing, or a garden is a thing. The rain was a season, and a sound, and a smell, and a memory, and her grandmother had left it to her in a letter, which Adaeze found on the kitchen table, in an envelope with her name on it, in her grandmother's handwriting, which was careful, and slow, and which said: "My dear Adaeze, I leave you the house, and the garden, and the rain. The house you will know what to do with. The garden you will learn. The rain — the rain you must listen to, because the rain knows things, and it will tell you, if you listen, and it will not tell you, if you do not. Your grandmother, who loved you, and who is now with the rain."

Adaeze was twenty-nine years old, and she lived in the city, and she worked in an office, with air conditioning, and she had not lived in her grandmother's house since she was a child, and she had not thought about the rain, not really, not in years, because in the city, the rain was an inconvenience, something that made the traffic worse, and the clothes wet, and the day longer. But her grandmother had left her the rain, and Adaeze, who had loved her grandmother, and who had not been there when she died, because the city was far away, and the work was important, and the excuses were easy, decided to go back, to the house on the hill, and to listen to the rain, and to see what it knew.

She arrived in June, at the beginning of the rainy season, and the house was as she remembered it, small, and cool, and smelling of woodsmoke, and of mangoes, and the garden was overgrown, and the mango tree was larger than she remembered, and the rain — the rain was already there, falling, softly, on the tin roof, singing, the way her grandmother had said it sang, and Adaeze stood on the veranda, with a cup of tea, the way her grandmother had stood, and she listened, and the rain said nothing, at first, because rain does not speak at first, to strangers, and Adaeze was a stranger, now, in her grandmother's house, after ten years in the city, and the rain was waiting, to see if she would stay.

She stayed. She stayed for a week, and then for a month, and then for the whole rainy season, and she learned the garden, slowly, the way her grandmother had said she would learn it, by doing, and by failing, and by doing again. She learned the yams, and the plantains, and she learned the mango tree, which dropped its fruit in July, and which fed her, and the neighbours, and the birds, and everyone, for weeks, and she learned the rain, which fell every afternoon, at three o'clock, as regular as a clock, and which sang on the tin roof, and which smelled of earth, and of green things, and which, Adaeze began to understand, was not just weather, but a kind of company, and a kind of memory, and a kind of inheritance, which is to say, a thing that is given to you, not because you have earned it, but because you are loved, and because the giver wants you to have it, and to keep it, and to pass it on.

As she worked in the garden, Adaeze remembered. She remembered the summers, when she was a child, when she came to stay with her grandmother, for the whole of August, and her grandmother taught her to listen to the rain, sitting on the veranda, with two cups of tea, one for each of them, although Adaeze was only eight, and the tea was mostly milk, and mostly sugar, and her grandmother said, "Listen, Adaeze. Listen to the rain. It is telling you a story. It is telling you about the sky, and about the earth, and about the things that grow, and the things that do not, and if you listen carefully, it will tell you about yourself, too."

Adaeze had listened, then, because children listen, when someone they love tells them to listen, and she had heard the rain, on the tin roof, and she had thought it was a story, and she had fallen asleep, on the veranda, with her head on her grandmother's lap, and her grandmother had covered her with a cloth, and had sat there, all evening, watching the sky, and the rain, and her granddaughter, sleeping, and that, Adaeze understood now, was what love was: sitting, and watching, and listening, and not needing anything else.

She remembered the mango tree, and how she had climbed it, when she was ten, and how her grandmother had stood below, and said, "Careful, Adaeze. The tree is old, and it is strong, but you are young, and you are not, and if you fall, I will catch you, but I would rather not have to, because I am old, and catching is hard work." Adaeze had not fallen. She had climbed to the top, and she had sat there, among the leaves, and she had eaten a mango, warm from the sun, and she had looked out, over the hill, and over the village, and over the whole world, and she had thought: this is the highest place in the world, and I am in it, and my grandmother is below me, watching, and that is enough, and that will always be enough.

She remembered the last summer, when she was seventeen, and she had come to say goodbye, because she was going to the city, to study, and to work, and her grandmother had given her a mango, and had said, "Take this, Adaeze. Eat it in the city, and remember the tree, and remember the rain, and remember me, and come back, when you can, because the house will be here, and the garden will be here, and the rain will be here, and I will be here, as long as I am here, and after that, the rain will be here, for me, and you must listen to it, because it will tell you what I would have told you, if I were still here to tell it."

Adaeze had eaten the mango, on the bus, to the city, and she had cried, quietly, where no one could see, and she had not come back, not for ten years, not until the letter, on the kitchen table, in her grandmother's handwriting, which said: "I leave you the house, and the garden, and the rain," and now she was back, and she was listening, and the rain was telling her, every afternoon, at three o'clock, on the tin roof, the story her grandmother had told her, when she was eight, and the story was this: you are loved, and you are home, and you are where you belong, and the rain knows it, and the mango tree knows it, and the house knows it, and you know it, too, if you listen.

In August, a man came to the house. His name was Chidi, and he was a farmer, from the next village, and he had known her grandmother, and he had come to ask if Adaeze wanted to sell the house, and the garden, because a developer, from the city, wanted to buy the land, and build houses on it, and Chidi, who was an honest man, and who did not like developers, said, "Adaeze, I have come to tell you, because I think you should know, and because your grandmother would have wanted you to know, that the developer has offered a great deal of money, and that many people in the village have sold, and that if you sell, you will be rich, and if you do not sell, you will be — well, you will be what your grandmother was, which is not rich, but which is something else, and I do not know what to call it, except that it is a good thing, and that I think you should think about it, before you decide."

The developer came himself, a week later. His name was Mr. Okafor, and he wore a suit, in the village, in the rain, and he carried an umbrella, and a briefcase, and he said, "Miss Adaeze, I will be frank. Your land is worth a great deal. I will pay you twice what it is worth. You can go back to the city, and live well, and forget about this hill, and this house, and this garden, which is, if you will forgive me, a great deal of work, for very little return."

Adaeze looked at him. She looked at his suit, and his umbrella, and his briefcase, and she said, "Mr. Okafor, have you ever listened to the rain, on a tin roof?"

Mr. Okafor blinked. "I beg your pardon?"

"The rain," Adaeze said. "On a tin roof. It sings. My grandmother said it sings, and she was right. It sings, every afternoon, at three o'clock, and it tells you a story, about the sky, and the earth, and yourself, and if you have never heard it, then you do not know what you are asking me to sell, and if you have heard it, and you still want to buy it, then you do not understand what it is, and either way, the answer is no. The house is not for sale. The garden is not for sale. The rain is not for sale. Good day, Mr. Okafor. And take your umbrella with you. It is going to rain, at three o'clock, as it always does, and you will want it, on the road back to the city."

Mr. Okafor left. He did not come back. And Adaeze, standing on the veranda, with a cup of tea, listening to the rain, which came at three o'clock, as it always did, thought: my grandmother was right. The rain knows things. And one of the things it knows is how to say no, politely, and firmly, and finally, to a man in a suit, with an umbrella, and a briefcase, who thinks that everything is for sale, and who is wrong, about the things that matter most.

Adaeze thought about it. She thought about the money, which would be a great deal, and which would pay for a flat in the city, and for a car, and for a life that was easier, and cleaner, and drier, than the life on the hill, with the tin roof, and the garden, and the rain. And she thought about her grandmother, sitting on the veranda, with a cup of tea, watching the sky, and she thought about the mango tree, which was older than her, and older than her grandmother, and which would outlive them all, and she thought about the rain, which sang on the tin roof, every afternoon, at three o'clock, and she thought about the letter, on the kitchen table, in her grandmother's handwriting, which said: "The rain you must listen to, because the rain knows things, and it will tell you, if you listen."

She listened. She went out, onto the veranda, in the rain, and she stood there, getting wet, and she listened, and the rain said, in the way that rain says things, not in words, but in sound, and in smell, and in the feeling of water on skin: "Stay. Stay, and keep the house, and keep the garden, and keep me, because I am yours, and you are mine, and we belong to each other, and to this hill, and to this mango tree, and to your grandmother, who is now with me, and who is listening, too, and who is proud of you, for coming back, and for staying, and for listening."

Adaeze went back inside. She dried herself. She made tea. She sat on the veranda, the way her grandmother had sat, and she said to Chidi, who was waiting, patiently, in the doorway: "Tell the developer no. Tell him the house is not for sale, and the garden is not for sale, and the rain is not for sale, because some things are not for sale, and these are three of them, and I am staying, and I am keeping them, and I am going to learn the garden, and I am going to listen to the rain, and I am going to be, for the rest of my life, the woman who inherited the rain, and who kept it, and who passed it on."

Chidi smiled. He was an honest man, and he was glad, and he said, "Your grandmother would be proud, Adaeze. She always said you would come back. She always said the rain would bring you back, because the rain knows things, and it knows who belongs to it, and who does not, and you, Adaeze, you belong to it, and it belongs to you, and that is the best inheritance there is."

Adaeze stayed. She stayed through the rainy season, and through the dry season, and through another rainy season, and she learned the garden, and she learned the rain, and she learned the house, and she learned herself, in a way she had not learned herself in the city, and in October, when the rains ended, and the sky cleared, and the mango tree dropped its last fruit, Adaeze sat on the veranda, with a cup of tea, and she looked at the sky, and she thought about her grandmother, who was now with the rain, and she thought about the rain, which would come back, in June, as it always did, and she thought about the house, and the garden, and the mango tree, and she thought: this is what an inheritance is. Not a house, or a garden, or money, but a place, and a sound, and a smell, and a memory, and a promise, that you will keep it, and that you will pass it on, and that the rain, which knows things, will tell you, if you listen, and you will listen, because listening is the least you can do, for a grandmother who loved you, and who left you the rain.

ABBREV = {"st", "mr", "mrs", "ms", "dr", "jr", "sr", "capt", "lt", "gen", "col", "rev", "hon", "prof", "fig", "no", "vol", "pp", "etc", "vs", "ave", "blvd", "u.s", "e.g", "i.e", "m", "mm", "mme", "fr", "b.c", "a.d"}
def split_sentences(text):
    text = " ".join(text.split())
    bounds = []
    for m in re.finditer(r'[.!?]["\u201d\u2019]?\s+', text):
        before = text[:m.start()].rstrip()
        tok = before.split()[-1].lower().rstrip(".") if before.split() else ""
        if tok in ABBREV:
            continue
        bounds.append(m.end())
    out, start = [], 0
    for b in bounds:

        start = b
    tail = text[start:].strip()
    if tail:
        out.append(tail)
    return [s for s in out if s]

The rain was a season, and a sound, and a smell, and a memory, and her grandmother had left it to her in a letter, which Adaeze found on the kitchen table, in an envelope with her name on it, in her grandmother\'s handwriting, which was careful, and slow, and which said: "My dear Adaeze, I leave you the house, and the garden, and the rain. The house you will know what to do with. The garden you will learn. The rain — the rain you must listen to, because the rain knows things, and it will tell you, if you listen, and it will not tell you, if you do not. Your grandmother, who loved you, and who is now with the rain."\n\nAdaeze was twenty-nine years old, and she lived in the city, and she worked in an office, with air conditioning, and she had not lived in her grandmother\'s house since she was a child, and she had not thought about the rain, not really, not in years, because in the city, the rain was an inconvenience, something that made the traffic worse, and the clothes wet, and the day longer. But her grandmother had left her the rain, and Adaeze, who had loved her grandmother, and who had not been there when she died, because the city was far away, and the work was important, and the excuses were easy, decided to go back, to the house on the hill, and to listen to the rain, and to see what it knew.\n\nShe arrived in June, at the beginning of the rainy season, and the house was as she remembered it, small, and cool, and smelling of woodsmoke, and of mangoes, and the garden was overgrown, and the mango tree was larger than she remembered, and the rain — the rain was already there, falling, softly, on the tin roof, singing, the way her grandmother had said it sang, and Adaeze stood on the veranda, with a cup of tea, the way her grandmother had stood, and she listened, and the rain said nothing, at first, because rain does not speak at first, to strangers, and Adaeze was a stranger, now, in her grandmother\'s house, after ten years in the city, and the rain was waiting, to see if she would stay.\n\nShe stayed. She stayed for a week, and then for a month, and then for the whole rainy season, and she learned the garden, slowly, the way her grandmother had said she would learn it, by doing, and by failing, and by doing again. She learned the yams, and the plantains, and she learned the mango tree, which dropped its fruit in July, and which fed her, and the neighbours, and the birds, and everyone, for weeks, and she learned the rain, which fell every afternoon, at three o\'clock, as regular as a clock, and which sang on the tin roof, and which smelled of earth, and of green things, and which, Adaeze began to understand, was not just weather, but a kind of company, and a kind of memory, and a kind of inheritance, which is to say, a thing that is given to you, not because you have earned it, but because you are loved, and because the giver wants you to have it, and to keep it, and to pass it on.\n\nAs she worked in the garden, Adaeze remembered. She remembered the summers, when she was a child, when she came to stay with her grandmother, for the whole of August, and her grandmother taught her to listen to the rain, sitting on the veranda, with two cups of tea, one for each of them, although Adaeze was only eight, and the tea was mostly milk, and mostly sugar, and her grandmother said, "Listen, Adaeze. Listen to the rain. It is telling you a story. It is telling you about the sky, and about the earth, and about the things that grow, and the things that do not, and if you listen carefully, it will tell you about yourself, too."\n\nAdaeze had listened, then, because children listen, when someone they love tells them to listen, and she had heard the rain, on the tin roof, and she had thought it was a story, and she had fallen asleep, on the veranda, with her head on her grandmother\'s lap, and her grandmother had covered her with a cloth, and had sat there, all evening, watching the sky, and the rain, and her granddaughter, sleeping, and that, Adaeze understood now, was what love was: sitting, and watching, and listening, and not needing anything else.\n\nShe remembered the mango tree, and how she had climbed it, when she was ten, and how her grandmother had stood below, and said, "Careful, Adaeze. The tree is old, and it is strong, but you are young, and you are not, and if you fall, I will catch you, but I would rather not have to, because I am old, and catching is hard work." Adaeze had not fallen. She had climbed to the top, and she had sat there, among the leaves, and she had eaten a mango, warm from the sun, and she had looked out, over the hill, and over the village, and over the whole world, and she had thought: this is the highest place in the world, and I am in it, and my grandmother is below me, watching, and that is enough, and that will always be enough.\n\nShe remembered the last summer, when she was seventeen, and she had come to say goodbye, because she was going to the city, to study, and to work, and her grandmother had given her a mango, and had said, "Take this, Adaeze. Eat it in the city, and remember the tree, and remember the rain, and remember me, and come back, when you can, because the house will be here, and the garden will be here, and the rain will be here, and I will be here, as long as I am here, and after that, the rain will be here, for me, and you must listen to it, because it will tell you what I would have told you, if I were still here to tell it."\n\nAdaeze had eaten the mango, on the bus, to the city, and she had cried, quietly, where no one could see, and she had not come back, not for ten years, not until the letter, on the kitchen table, in her grandmother\'s handwriting, which said: "I leave you the house, and the garden, and the rain," and now she was back, and she was listening, and the rain was telling her, every afternoon, at three o\'clock, on the tin roof, the story her grandmother had told her, when she was eight, and the story was this: you are loved, and you are home, and you are where you belong, and the rain knows it, and the mango tree knows it, and the house knows it, and you know it, too, if you listen.\n\nIn August, a man came to the house. His name was Chidi, and he was a farmer, from the next village, and he had known her grandmother, and he had come to ask if Adaeze wanted to sell the house, and the garden, because a developer, from the city, wanted to buy the land, and build houses on it, and Chidi, who was an honest man, and who did not like developers, said, "Adaeze, I have come to tell you, because I think you should know, and because your grandmother would have wanted you to know, that the developer has offered a great deal of money, and that many people in the village have sold, and that if you sell, you will be rich, and if you do not sell, you will be — well, you will be what your grandmother was, which is not rich, but which is something else, and I do not know what to call it, except that it is a good thing, and that I think you should think about it, before you decide."\n\nThe developer came himself, a week later. His name was Mr. Okafor, and he wore a suit, in the village, in the rain, and he carried an umbrella, and a briefcase, and he said, "Miss Adaeze, I will be frank. Your land is worth a great deal. I will pay you twice what it is worth. You can go back to the city, and live well, and forget about this hill, and this house, and this garden, which is, if you will forgive me, a great deal of work, for very little return."\n\nAdaeze looked at him. She looked at his suit, and his umbrella, and his briefcase, and she said, "Mr. Okafor, have you ever listened to the rain, on a tin roof?"\n\nMr. Okafor blinked. "I beg your pardon?"\n\n"The rain," Adaeze said. "On a tin roof. It sings. My grandmother said it sings, and she was right. The house is not for sale. The garden is not for sale. The rain is not for sale. Good day, Mr. Okafor. And take your umbrella with you. And Adaeze, standing on the veranda, with a cup of tea, listening to the rain, which came at three o\'clock, as it always did, thought: my grandmother was right. The rain knows things. And she thought about her grandmother, sitting on the veranda, with a cup of tea, watching the sky, and she thought about the mango tree, which was older than her, and older than her grandmother, and which would outlive them all, and she thought about the rain, which sang on the tin roof, every afternoon, at three o\'clock, and she thought about the letter, on the kitchen table, in her grandmother\'s handwriting, which said: "The rain you must listen to, because the rain knows things, and it will tell you, if you listen."\n\nShe listened. Inspector Ravi Menon, a railway policeman, investigates a train that leaves platform seven at eleven-forty every night and never arrives anywhere. Riding it, he finds passengers who have lost someone and are not ready to go home, and he discovers that he is one of them. A mystery about grief, trains, and the kindness of going nowhere.

An original Signature short story in the mystery genre, written for The Publishable Short Stories Database (Signature Edition) in 2026. It was created as a complete publishable work, with no prior publication and no model on any existing story.

JAH Signature (Justin Addam Higgins) is the Signature byline for original works in this database. This story is an original work, written for this edition.

The train's timetable is its theology: it leaves at eleven-forty because nowhere is where its passengers need to go, and it waits because waiting is the service it provides. The story opens with: “The night train to nowhere left the station at eleven-forty, every night, and no one knew where it went, and no one, except for Inspector Ravi Menon, cared enough to find out.” and closes with: “Let it run.” Across 27 paragraphs and 108 sentences, the opening promise and the closing line frame the whole arc, and the ending re-reads the beginning: what the first sentence sets in motion, the last sentence settles.

Full text

The night train to nowhere left the station at eleven-forty, every night, and no one knew where it went, and no one, except for Inspector Ravi Menon, cared enough to find out.

Ravi had been a railway policeman for twenty years, and he had seen many strange things on the railways: a man who tried to smuggle a tiger in a suitcase; a woman who had lived on a train for three years, moving from carriage to carriage, because she had nowhere else to go; a stationmaster who had stolen the station clock, because he said it was the only thing in the station that told the truth. But the night train to nowhere was the strangest thing he had ever seen, because it was a train, with an engine, and carriages, and passengers, and a timetable, and it left the station every night, at eleven-forty, and it never arrived anywhere, and no one, on any other station, had ever seen it arrive.

Ravi first noticed it on a Tuesday, in October, when he was doing the rounds, late, and he saw a train on platform seven, which was a platform that had not been used in years, and the train was old, and green, and it had steam coming from its engine, although no steam trains had run on that line in fifty years, and there were people on it, sitting in the carriages, reading newspapers, and drinking tea, and looking out of the windows, as if they were going somewhere, and Ravi, who was a practical man, and who did not believe in ghosts, or in magic, or in trains that went nowhere, went to the ticket office, and asked, "What train is that, on platform seven?"

The ticket clerk, a young man named Dev, who had worked at the station for two years, and who had never seen the train before, said, "I don't know, Inspector. It is not on the timetable. It is not on the board. It is not —" He stopped, and he looked out of the window, at platform seven, and he said, "Inspector. It is gone."

Ravi looked. Platform seven was empty. The train was gone. There was no smoke, and no steam, and no sound, and the platform was as it had always been, empty, and dusty, and unused, and Ravi, who had seen the train, with his own eyes, and who had seen the people on it, reading their newspapers, stood there, and said, "Dev. I saw a train. Did you see it?"

Dev nodded, slowly. "I saw it, Inspector. I saw it too. And now it is gone. And I do not know where it went, or how, or why."

Ravi investigated. He checked the records. He checked the timetables, going back fifty years. He checked the station logs. He asked the old railwaymen, who had worked at the station for forty years, and who remembered everything, and they said, "Oh, yes, Inspector. The night train. It has always been there. It leaves at eleven-forty, every night, and it goes nowhere, and it comes from nowhere, and the people on it — well, the people on it are the people who have nowhere to go, and who have always had nowhere to go, and who ride the train, because riding is better than waiting, and waiting is better than nothing."

Ravi went to the archive, in the basement of the station, where the old timetables were kept, in boxes, covered in dust, and he searched, for hours, through timetables from 1954, and 1962, and 1971, and he found it, in a timetable from 1954, on page forty-seven: a train, listed as "The Night Service", departing platform seven, at eleven-forty, destination: "—", and in the margin, in pencil, in handwriting that was old, and careful, someone had written: "For those who need to go nowhere. Do not cancel. Do not question. Let it run."

Ravi showed it to Dev, the ticket clerk, and Dev said, "Inspector, who wrote that? And why is the destination a dash? And why does it say 'do not cancel'?"

"I do not know," Ravi said. "But I am going to find out. And the way to find out, Dev, is to ride the train, and to ask the people on it, and to listen, because listening is what a policeman does, when the records do not have the answer, and the timetables do not have the answer, and the only answer is on the train, in the night, going nowhere."

Dev looked at him, and he said, "Inspector. Are you afraid?"

Ravi thought about it. He was a practical man, and he had been a railway policeman for twenty years, and he had seen many strange things, and he was not afraid of ghosts, or of magic, or of trains, but he was afraid of something else, something he had not named, in ten years, since his wife had died, and he said, "Yes, Dev. I am afraid. I am afraid of what I will find on that train, and I am afraid of what I will not find, and I am afraid that I will get on, and I will not want to get off, and that is the most frightening thing of all, for a policeman, who is supposed to investigate, and to file a report, and to go home."

"Then I will come with you," Dev said. "Not as a policeman. As a witness. And if you do not want to get off, I will remind you, and I will help you get off, and we will file the report together, and we will go home, together, in the morning, when the sun is up, and the train is gone, and platform seven is empty, and dusty, and unused, as it has always been, except at eleven-forty, every night, when it is not."

One of the old railwaymen, a man named Thomas, who was eighty-two, and who had been a driver, once, said, "I drove that train, Inspector. Once. Forty years ago. I was young, and I was foolish, and I took the job, because no one else would take it, and I drove it, from platform seven, at eleven-forty, and I drove it all night, through stations that were not on any map, and past towns that were not on any timetable, and the passengers — they were quiet, and they were kind, and they thanked me, when they got off, although I never saw where they got off, because they got off in the dark, and in the morning, I was back at the station, and the train was on platform seven, and I never drove it again, because once is enough, for a train like that, and because some journeys are not meant to be taken twice."

Ravi did not believe him. Ravi was a practical man. But he went to platform seven, on the next night, at eleven-thirty, and he waited, and at eleven-forty, the train came, green, and old, with steam, and with people, reading newspapers, and drinking tea, and Ravi got on it, because a policeman investigates, and investigating means getting on the train, even if the train goes nowhere, especially if the train goes nowhere.

The train left the station. It went through the dark, and Ravi looked out of the window, and he saw stations, going past, stations he did not recognise, with names he had never seen, and towns, with lights, and fields, and rivers, and the train went on, and on, and the passengers sat, quietly, reading, and drinking tea, and Ravi went to the buffet car, and he bought a cup of tea, from a man who was old, and kind, and who said, "Inspector. You are new. Welcome. Would you like a newspaper?"

Ravi took the newspaper. It was dated 1954. He looked at the man, and he said, "Where does this train go?"

The man smiled. "Nowhere, Inspector. That is the point. This train goes nowhere, because nowhere is where its passengers need to go. They are the people who have lost something, or someone, and who cannot go home, and who cannot go forward, and so they ride, in the night, in the dark, until they are ready, and when they are ready, they get off, and they go home, or they go forward, and they do not come back, because they do not need to, any more."

Ravi looked around the carriage. He saw a woman, with a photograph in her hand, of a child, who was not there. He saw a man, with a suitcase, that was empty. He saw an old woman, with a letter, that she had never sent. And he understood, suddenly, that the train was not a mystery, in the way that a crime is a mystery, but a kindness, in the way that a kindness is a mystery, when you do not expect it, and when you need it, and when it comes, in the night, on platform seven, at eleven-forty, green, and old, with steam.

"How long do they ride?" Ravi asked.

"As long as they need to," the man said. "Some ride for a night. Some ride for a year. Some ride for a lifetime. And some — some get off, and come back, years later, to ride again, because life is long, and loss is long, and sometimes, you need the train again, and the train is always there, on platform seven, at eleven-forty, waiting, because that is what trains do, and that is what this train does, better than any other train in the world: it waits, and it goes nowhere, and it takes you with it, until you are ready to go somewhere."

Ravi rode the train all night. He talked to the passengers. He listened to their stories. He drank tea. He read the newspaper, from 1954, which had news in it that was old, and new, all at once, because news, on the night train, is not about what happened, but about what matters, and what matters does not change, not in fifty years, not ever.

He talked to the woman with the photograph. Her name was Meera, and the photograph was of her daughter, who had died, five years ago, in an accident, and Meera said, "I ride the train, Inspector, because at home, every room has her in it, and every silence is her silence, and on the train, the silence is different, because it is shared, and because the other passengers understand, and because the train goes nowhere, and going nowhere is the only place I can go, where I do not have to be a mother who has lost a child, but can simply be a woman, on a train, with a photograph, going nowhere, until I am ready to go somewhere."

He talked to the man with the empty suitcase. His name was Joseph, and the suitcase was empty because he had packed it, to leave his wife, and then he had not left, and then she had left him, and he had kept the suitcase, empty, because it was the only thing he had packed, and because it reminded him of the moment when he had almost been brave, and almost been free, and he said, "I ride the train, Inspector, because I am still packing, in a way, and I am still deciding, and the train gives me time, and time is what I need, to decide whether to go, or to stay, or to do something else entirely, which I have not thought of yet, but which I will think of, on the train, in the night, going nowhere."

He talked to the old woman with the letter. Her name was Grace, and she was eighty-nine, and the letter was to her sister, who had died, sixty years ago, and to whom Grace had never written, because they had quarrelled, when they were young, over a man, and over a house, and over nothing, really, and Grace said, "I ride the train, Inspector, because I am going to post the letter, one day, although there is no one to post it to, and although the address is a house that no longer stands, and I ride the train, because on the train, the letter is not a letter that was never sent, but a letter that is still travelling, and as long as it is travelling, it is not too late, and as long as it is not too late, I can still say what I should have said, sixty years ago, which is: I am sorry, and I love you, and the quarrel was not worth it, and nothing was worth it, except you."

Ravi listened to them all. He listened, and he understood, and he thought about his wife, who had died, ten years ago, and whom he had not mourned, properly, because policemen do not mourn, they investigate, and they file reports, and they go home, and they sleep, and he thought: I am like them. I am a passenger, too. I have been a passenger for ten years, and I did not know it, until tonight, on this train, going nowhere, with a cup of tea, and a newspaper from 1954, and three strangers, who have taught me, without trying, what the train is for, and what I am for, and what I need to do, which is to mourn, and to ride, and to wait, until I am ready, to go somewhere, again. And in the morning, when the train came back to the station, and the sun was rising, and platform seven was empty, and dusty, and unused, Ravi got off, and he went to his office, and he wrote a report, which said: "The night train to nowhere: investigated. No crime committed. No passengers missing. No train missing. The train goes nowhere, and it takes people who need to go nowhere, and it brings them back, when they are ready. Case closed."

He filed the report. He went home. He slept. And the next night, at eleven-thirty, he went to platform seven, and he waited, and at eleven-forty, the train came, and Ravi got on it, not as a policeman, but as a passenger, because Ravi, who had been a railway policeman for twenty years, and who had seen many strange things, had also lost someone, once, a wife, who had died, ten years ago, and who he had not mourned, properly, because policemen do not mourn, they investigate, and they file reports, and they go home, and they sleep, and Ravi, on the night train, with a cup of tea, and a newspaper from 1954, began, at last, to mourn, and to ride, and to wait, until he was ready, to go somewhere, again. And Dev, who had come with him, and who had waited, and who had watched, wrote in the station log, in pencil, in the margin, beside the entry for platform seven: "The train runs. It always runs. Let it run.

ABBREV = {"st", "mr", "mrs", "ms", "dr", "jr", "sr", "capt", "lt", "gen", "col", "rev", "hon", "prof", "fig", "no", "vol", "pp", "etc", "vs", "ave", "blvd", "u.s", "e.g", "i.e", "m", "mm", "mme", "fr", "b.c", "a.d"}
def split_sentences(text):
    text = " ".join(text.split())
    bounds = []
    for m in re.finditer(r'[.!?]["\u201d\u2019]?\s+', text):
        before = text[:m.start()].rstrip()
        tok = before.split()[-1].lower().rstrip(".") if before.split() else ""
        if tok in ABBREV:
            continue
        bounds.append(m.end())
    out, start = [], 0
    for b in bounds:
        out.append(text[start:b].strip())
        start = b
    tail = text[start:].strip()
    if tail:
        out.append(tail)
    return [s for s in out if s]
