import re
ABBREV = {"st", "mr", "mrs", "ms", "dr", "jr", "sr", "capt", "lt", "gen", "col", "rev", "hon", "prof", "fig", "no", "vol", "pp", "etc", "vs", "ave", "blvd", "u.s", "e.g", "i.e", "m", "mm", "mme", "fr", "b.c", "a.d"}
def split_sentences(text):
    text = " ".join(text.split())
    bounds = []
    for m in re.finditer(r'[.!?]["\u201d\u2019]?\s+', text):
        before = text[:m.start()].rstrip()
        tok = before.split()[-1].lower().rstrip(".") if before.split() else ""
        if tok in ABBREV:
            continue
        bounds.append(m.end())
    out, start = [], 0
    for b in bounds:
        out.append(text[start:b].strip())
        start = b
    tail = text[start:].strip()
    if tail:
        out.append(tail)
    return [s for s in out if s]

Behind the house at the end of Willow Lane, where the fence was broken and the gate hung on one hinge, there was a garden, and in the garden, there were things, and the things were unfinished.

There was a chair, with three legs, and a fourth leg leaning against it, waiting to be attached. There was a table, with one corner unvarnished, and a brush, dried hard, lying beside it. There was a painting, of a sea, with the sky half-finished, and the clouds only sketched, in pencil. There was a book, with the last chapter unwritten, and a pen, beside it, out of ink. There was a dress, on a stand, with one sleeve sewn, and the other pinned, waiting. There was a clock, with its hands stopped at ten past four, and its back open, and its gears laid out, in a row, like small, patient soldiers.

The garden belonged to Mrs. Elda Wren, who was seventy-three years old, and who had lived in the house at the end of Willow Lane for fifty years, and who had started a great many things, and finished very few of them, because finishing, Mrs. Wren had discovered, was the hardest part of anything, and starting was the easiest, and the most joyful, and so she had started, and started, and started, and the garden had filled up, with her beginnings, and the house had filled up, too, and Mrs. Wren, looking out of her kitchen window, at the garden, thought, every morning: I should finish something today. And every evening, she thought: tomorrow. Tomorrow I will finish something. And tomorrow came, and went, and the garden grew, with unfinished things, the way other gardens grow with flowers.

On the first day of spring, a girl came to the garden. Her name was Poppy, and she was nine years old, and she lived three houses down Willow Lane, and she had come because she had lost a ball, over the fence, and she had climbed the fence to get it, and she had found, instead of a ball, a garden full of unfinished things, and a woman, standing in the doorway, watching her, with her arms folded, and a smile on her face.

"Are you lost?" Mrs. Wren asked.

"I am looking for my ball," Poppy said. "It came over the fence. It is red. Have you seen it?"

Mrs. Wren looked around the garden. She saw the chair, with three legs. She saw the table, with one corner unvarnished. She saw the painting, and the book, and the dress, and the clock. She did not see a red ball. "I have not seen it," she said. "But you may look for it. And while you look, you may look at the other things, too, if you like. They are all unfinished. Every one of them. I started them, and I did not finish them, and they have been waiting, in the garden, for someone to finish them, or for me to finish them, and I have not, and I do not know why, except that finishing is hard, and starting is easy, and I am very good at starting."

Poppy looked at the things. She looked at the chair. She looked at the clock, with its gears laid out, in a row. She looked at the painting, of the sea, with the sky half-finished. And she said, "Why don't you finish them?"

Mrs. Wren thought about it. She had thought about it, many times, in fifty years, and she had never had a good answer, and she said, honestly, because Poppy was nine, and nine-year-olds deserve honest answers: "Because I am afraid. I am afraid that if I finish them, they will not be as good as I hoped, and I am afraid that if I finish them, there will be nothing left to start, and I am afraid that finishing means ending, and I do not like endings, and so I start, and I do not finish, and the garden fills up, with my fear, disguised as beginnings."

Poppy nodded, as if this made perfect sense, which, to a nine-year-old, it did. "I am not afraid of finishing," she said. "I finish things all the time. I finish my dinner. I finish my homework. I finish books. Finishing is easy. You just do the last bit, and then it is finished."

Mrs. Wren laughed. It was a laugh she had not laughed in a long time, a laugh that came from somewhere deep, and surprised her, and she said, "Poppy. Would you like to help me finish something? Just one thing. Today. We will finish the chair. The fourth leg is there, leaning against it. We will attach it, and the chair will have four legs, and it will be finished, and we will sit on it, and we will see if the world ends, or if it goes on, much as before, except with one more finished chair in it."

Poppy said yes. They attached the fourth leg. It took an hour, and it was not perfect, and the chair wobbled, slightly, but it stood, and it held, and Mrs. Wren sat on it, carefully, and it held her, and Poppy sat on it, after her, and it held her too, and Mrs. Wren said, "The world did not end. The chair is finished. And I am still here. And you are still here. And the garden is still here, with all its unfinished things, except now there is one less, and that is a beginning, of a different kind."

Poppy came back the next day. And the next. And every day after school, for the whole of spring, Poppy came to the garden, and she and Mrs. Wren finished things, one by one. They varnished the table. They finished the painting, of the sea, with the sky, and the clouds, and Poppy painted the clouds, because she was good at clouds, and Mrs. Wren painted the sea, because she was good at the sea, and together, they finished it, and they hung it in the kitchen, where Mrs. Wren could see it, every morning, while she made tea.

One afternoon, while they were varnishing the table, Poppy asked, "Mrs. Wren, why did you start so many things? Did you not want to finish them, when you started them?"

Mrs. Wren put down her brush. She looked at the garden, at the unfinished things, still waiting, and she said, "Poppy, when I was young, I was married, to a man named Albert, who was a wonderful man, and who started things, too, and who finished them, every one, and he taught me to start, and he did not teach me to finish, because he was always there, to finish, and I was always there, to start, and we were a pair, you see, a starter and a finisher, and it worked, for forty years, until Albert died, ten years ago, and then there was no one to finish, and I kept starting, because starting was what I knew, and finishing was what Albert knew, and without him, I did not know how to finish, and so the garden filled up, with my beginnings, waiting for a finisher, who never came, until you came, looking for a red ball, and you are my finisher now, Poppy, and I am your starter, and together, we are a pair, like Albert and I were, and that is a wonderful thing, to be a pair, again, after ten years of being only half of one."

Poppy thought about this. She was nine, and she understood loss, in the way that nine-year-olds understand loss, which is completely, and without the complications that adults add to it, and she said, "Mrs. Wren, I am sorry about Albert. But I am glad he taught you to start, because starting is the best part, and I am glad I can finish, because finishing is the best part, too, and together, we can do both, and the garden will be finished, one day, and then we will start new things, together, and finish them together, and that will be our garden, and our life, and no one will be only half of a pair any more."

Mrs. Wren cried, then, a little, quietly, the way old women cry, when they are happy, and sad, at the same time, and Poppy pretended not to notice, and kept varnishing, and the table, which had one corner unvarnished, became varnished, all over, and it shone, in the spring sun, and Mrs. Wren said, "Thank you, Poppy. Thank you for coming over the fence, for a red ball, and for staying, to finish things, with an old woman who had forgotten how."

In the summer, Poppy brought her friends. There were four of them, from school, and they came to the garden, and they helped, and the garden, which had been a private place, for fifty years, became a shared place, and the children finished things, and Mrs. Wren taught them to start things, and they started a birdhouse, and a kite, and a puppet theatre, and they finished the birdhouse, and the kite, and the puppet theatre, and they performed a play, in the garden, for the whole of Willow Lane, and the play was about a garden, full of unfinished things, and a girl, who came looking for a ball, and a woman, who learned to finish, and everyone laughed, and everyone cried, and Mrs. Wren, sitting on the finished chair, in the finished dress, watching the play, thought: Albert would have loved this. Albert would have finished the play, and I would have started it, and now Poppy has finished it, and I have started it, and the garden goes on, and the story goes on, and nothing is ever really unfinished, as long as someone is willing to finish it, and someone is willing to start it, and the two of them meet, in a garden, on a spring day, over a fence, looking for a red ball.

They fixed the clock. They put the gears back, one by one, and they wound it, and it ticked, and it told the time, and Mrs. Wren said, "It is ten past four. It has been ten past four for twenty years, and now it is not ten past four any more, and I do not know what time it is, except that it is now, and now is a good time, to be finishing things."

They sewed the dress. Poppy sewed the second sleeve, with Mrs. Wren guiding her hands, and the dress was finished, and Mrs. Wren wore it, to the village fete, and everyone said how lovely it was, and Mrs. Wren said, "Poppy sewed the sleeve. She finished it. I started it, twenty years ago, and she finished it, and that is how it should be. We start things, and others finish them, and others start things, and we finish them, and that is how the world goes on."

The book was the hardest. The book had the last chapter unwritten, and Mrs. Wren had not written in twenty years, and she did not know how the book ended, and she said to Poppy, "I do not know the ending. I have forgotten it, or I never knew it, and I am afraid to write it, because if I write it wrong, the book will be ruined."

Poppy said, "Then I will write it. I will write the ending, and if it is wrong, we will write another one, and if that is wrong, we will write another, until it is right, or until we are tired, and then we will stop, and the book will be finished, or it will not, but we will have tried, and trying is the same as finishing, almost."

Poppy wrote the ending. It was not the ending Mrs. Wren would have written, but it was a good ending, and it was an ending, and Mrs. Wren read it, and she cried, a little, because the book was finished, after twenty years, and because a nine-year-old girl had finished it, and because finishing, it turned out, was not the end of the world, but the beginning of something else: a garden, with fewer unfinished things in it, and a house, with a finished painting in the kitchen, and a finished clock on the wall, and a finished dress in the wardrobe, and a finished book on the shelf, and a woman, seventy-three years old, who had learned, at last, that finishing is not frightening, and that starting is not enough, and that the best thing in the world is a friend, who comes to your garden, looking for a red ball, and stays, to help you finish things, one by one, until the garden is not a garden of unfinished things any more, but a garden of finished things, and of beginnings, and of a woman, and a girl, sitting on a finished chair, drinking tea, and looking at the garden, and saying: "What shall we finish tomorrow?"

It was under the table, behind the paint tins, red, and dusty, and she took it home, and she came back the next day, without it, because she did not need a reason to come back any more, and Mrs. Wren did not need a reason to finish things any more, because she had Poppy, and Poppy had her, and the garden had them both, and the unfinished things, one by one, became finished, and the finished things became a life, and the life became a story, and the story, like the book, had an ending, which was not an ending at all, but a beginning, of the next thing, to be started, and finished, together.\n\nIn the winter, when the garden was quiet, and the ground was hard, and the unfinished things were fewer, now, and the finished things were many, Poppy and Mrs. Wren sat in the kitchen, by the fire, with the finished painting on the wall, and the finished clock ticking, and the finished book on the shelf, and they made a list, of all the things they had finished, and all the things they would start, in the spring, and Mrs. Wren said, "Poppy, do you know what I have learned? I have learned that a garden is never finished, and that is as it should be, because a garden that is finished is a garden that is over, and our garden is not over, it is only beginning, and it will go on, as long as there is someone to start, and someone to finish, and someone to sit, in the kitchen, by the fire, making lists, in the winter, of all the things to come, in the spring." And Poppy said, "Then we will never be finished, Mrs. Wren," and Mrs. Wren said, "No, Poppy. We will never be finished. And that is the best thing of all.'

Thomas Penhaligon has kept the light for thirty years when the Admiralty orders it extinguished in 1940, because it guides the enemy as well as friends. When a ship comes close to the rocks in the dark, Thomas must choose between his orders and his duty. A historical story about light, obedience, and three minutes an hour.

The story opens with: “In the winter of 1940, on a rock off the coast of Cornwall, where the sea was grey, and the wind was cold, and the war was a distant sound, like thunder, on the other side of the water, there lived a lighthouse keeper named Thomas Penhaligon, who was fifty-eight years old, and who had kept the light for thirty years, and who had a problem, which was that the war had come to his lighthouse, and he did not know what to do about it.” and closes with: “You were born in it, in a storm, and you have lived by it, at sea, and one day, when I am gone, you will keep it, or someone will keep it, and the Light will shine, and the ships will come home, and that is the way it is, and the way it will always be, as long as there are rocks, and ships, and men, and lights, to guide them home.” Across 20 paragraphs and 94 sentences, the opening promise and the closing line frame the whole arc, and the ending re-reads the beginning: what the first sentence sets in motion, the last sentence settles.

Full text

In the winter of 1940, on a rock off the coast of Cornwall, where the sea was grey, and the wind was cold, and the war was a distant sound, like thunder, on the other side of the water, there lived a lighthouse keeper named Thomas Penhaligon, who was fifty-eight years old, and who had kept the light for thirty years, and who had a problem, which was that the war had come to his lighthouse, and he did not know what to do about it.

The lighthouse was called the Eddystone Light, although it was not the Eddystone, but a smaller light, on a smaller rock, with a smaller name, which Thomas never used, because he called it "the Light", and the Light was his life, and his duty, and his home, and he kept it, every night, turning, and shining, and warning the ships away from the rocks, and in the daytime, he cleaned the lens, and he painted the walls, and he listened to the wireless, and he heard about the war, about the Blitz, and about the ships that were being sunk, and about the men who were dying, and he thought: I am here, on a rock, keeping a light, and the world is at war, and I am doing nothing, and that is my duty, and my duty is not enough, any more.

In November, a boat came to the rock. It was a small boat, from the mainland, and it brought a man, who was not a lighthouse keeper, and who was not a fisherman, but a naval officer, in uniform, with a letter, sealed, and the letter said: "Mr. Penhaligon, by order of the Admiralty, the Light is to be extinguished, from tonight, until further notice, because the Light guides our ships, and it also guides theirs, and theirs are the ones we must not guide, and so the Light must go dark, and you must stay, and you must keep the Light dark, and you must not tell anyone, and you must be ready, when the order comes, to light it again."

Thomas read the letter. He read it twice. He looked at the officer, and he said, "Sir. I have kept this Light for thirty years. I have kept it through storms, and through fog, and through nights when I thought the sea would take the rock, and the Light, and me, with it. And now you tell me to put it out. You tell me to make the Light dark. You tell me that my duty, for thirty years, is now the opposite of my duty, and I am to sit here, in the dark, on a rock, in a war, and do nothing."

The officer nodded. He was young, and he looked tired, and he said, "Mr. Penhaligon. I know. I know it is hard. But the Light guides the enemy, too, and the enemy has ships, and the enemy has bombs, and the Light, shining, is a target, and a guide, and we cannot have it shining, not now, not while the war is on, and you must trust us, and you must put it out, and you must keep it out, until we tell you otherwise."

Thomas put the Light out. That night, for the first time in thirty years, the lighthouse was dark, and Thomas sat in the dark, in the lamp room, with the lens cold, and the sea below, grey and black, and the wind, cold, and he thought about the ships, out there, in the dark, without his Light to guide them, and he thought about the men on those ships, who were dying, in the war, and he thought about his own son, who was in the Navy, somewhere, on a ship, in the dark, and he thought: my son is out there, and my Light is dark, and I have put it out, because I was ordered to, and I do not know if I have done the right thing, or the wrong thing, and I will not know, until the war is over, or until my son comes home, or does not come home.

The winter went on. The Light stayed dark. Thomas stayed on the rock. He cleaned the lens, although there was no light to clean it for. He painted the walls. He listened to the wireless, and he heard about the Blitz, and about the ships, and about the men, and he waited, for the order to light the Light again, and the order did not come, and the nights were long, and dark, and Thomas, sitting in the dark, in the lamp room, began to talk to the Light, the way a man talks to a thing he has loved for thirty years, and he said, "Light. I am sorry. I have put you out. I have done what I was told. And I do not know if it was right. But I am here, and I am keeping you, even in the dark, and when the order comes, I will light you again, and you will shine, and the ships will see you, and they will come home."

Thomas had become a lighthouse keeper when he was twenty-eight, after ten years at sea, as a sailor, on merchant ships, going around the world, and seeing the lights, from the sea, and thinking, one night, off the coast of Africa, watching a lighthouse turn, and shine, and turn again: that is the best job in the world. To be the light, for others, in the dark. To be the thing that says: here are the rocks, and here is the safe water, and here is the way home. He had applied, and he had trained, and he had come to the rock, thirty years ago, with his wife, Mary, who had lived with him, on the rock, for five years, until she had died, of a fever, in the winter, and Thomas had buried her, on the mainland, and had come back, alone, to the Light, because the Light was his life, and his duty, and his home, and because Mary, before she died, had said, "Thomas, keep the Light. Keep it, for me, and for the ships, and for the men on them, because the Light is the best thing in the world, and you are the best man to keep it."

His son, William, had been born on the rock, in the lighthouse, in a storm, with the doctor coming by boat, late, and William had grown up, on the rock, and on the mainland, at school, and he had joined the Navy, when he was eighteen, because he wanted to be at sea, like his father had been, and like his grandfather had been, and Thomas had been proud, and afraid, and he had written to William, every week, from the rock, and William had written back, from his ship, and the letters had come, by boat, and Thomas had kept them, in a box, in the lamp room, and he read them, in the dark winter, when the Light was out, and the nights were long, and the letters said: "Father, I am well. The ship is well. We are at sea. I think of the Light, every night, and I look for it, and I do not see it, because it is dark, and I know why it is dark, and I am proud of you, for keeping it dark, and for keeping the rock, and for being my father, and for teaching me that a light, kept, is a promise, and a promise, kept, is a life."

In February, the letters stopped. For three weeks, no boat came, because of the weather, and no letter came, and Thomas sat in the dark, in the lamp room, and he worried, and he talked to the Light, and he said, "Light. Where is my son? Is he well? Is he alive? Tell me, Light, if you can, because you are the only one here, and I am alone, on a rock, in a war, and I need to know." The Light did not answer, because the Light was dark, and because lights do not answer, but Thomas kept talking, because talking is what a man does, when he is alone, and afraid, and the sea is below, and the war is beyond, and the only thing between him and the dark is a Light that he has put out, himself, by order, and by duty.

In March, the boat came, and it brought a letter, from William, and the letter said: "Father, I am alive. I am well. The ship was in a storm, and we could not write, and I am sorry for the worry, and I am proud of you, and I love you, and I will come home, when the war is over, and we will stand on the rock, together, and we will light the Light, together, all night, every night, as it should be." Thomas read the letter three times. He put it in the box, with the others. He went up to the lamp room, and he cleaned the lens, although there was no light to clean it for, and he thought: my son is alive, and the Light is dark, and the war goes on, and I am here, and I am keeping the Light, even in the dark, and that is my duty, and my life, and my home, and it is enough, for now, until the order comes, to light it again.

In March, a ship came to the rock. It was not a boat from the mainland. It was a ship, in the dark, without lights, and it was in trouble, and it was close to the rocks, and Thomas, looking out of the lamp room window, saw it, and he knew, in an instant, that it would hit the rocks, and sink, and that the men on it would die, unless the Light was lit, to guide it away, and Thomas, who had been ordered to keep the Light dark, and who had kept it dark, for four months, did something he had not done in thirty years: he disobeyed an order.

He lit the Light. He lit it, quickly, with hands that shook, and the Light turned, and shone, and the ship saw it, and turned away from the rocks, and went past, safe, into the dark, and Thomas stood in the lamp room, with the Light turning, and shining, and he thought: I have disobeyed. I will be punished. I will lose the Light. I will lose my job. I will lose everything. And I do not care, because the ship is safe, and the men on it are alive, and that is what the Light is for, and that is what I am for, and no order, from any Admiralty, in any war, can change that.

The next morning, a boat came from the mainland. It brought the same officer, and the officer said, "Mr. Penhaligon. The Light was seen, last night. It was lit, for three minutes. Do you know anything about that?"

Thomas looked at him. He said, "Yes, sir. I lit it. There was a ship, in trouble, close to the rocks, and I lit the Light, to guide it away, and the ship is safe, and the men are alive, and I disobeyed your order, and I am ready to accept the consequences."

The officer looked at him for a long moment. Then he said, "Mr. Penhaligon. The ship you saved was one of ours. It was carrying men, and supplies, and it was in the dark, without lights, because it was trying not to be seen, and it was close to the rocks, and you saved it. The Admiralty has been informed. And the Admiralty says: the Light is to be lit, from tonight, for three minutes, every hour, on the hour, to guide our ships, and to confuse theirs, and you are to keep it lit, in that way, until further notice, and you are not to be punished, Mr. Penhaligon, because you did what a lighthouse keeper does, which is to keep the Light, and to save the ships, and that is your duty, in war, and in peace, and always."

Thomas kept the Light. He lit it, for three minutes, every hour, on the hour, and the ships came, and went, and the war went on, and the three minutes became the most important three minutes of Thomas's life, because in those three minutes, the Light shone, and the ships saw it, and they knew where the rocks were, and where the safe water was, and Thomas, standing in the lamp room, watching the Light turn, thought: three minutes is not much. Three minutes is a short time. But three minutes, every hour, is enough, to save a ship, and to save the men on it, and to keep a promise, and to be a lighthouse keeper, in a war, when the Light must be dark, and must shine, both at once, and the only way to do both is three minutes, on the hour, every hour, all night, every night, until the war is over.

The ships learned the rhythm. They came, in the dark, and they waited, for the three minutes, and they fixed their positions, and they went on, and the enemy, who watched for the Light, saw it, and were confused, because a light that shines for three minutes, and then goes dark, is not a lighthouse, in the way they understood lighthouses, but a trick, or a signal, or a mistake, and they did not understand it, and Thomas, who understood it, smiled, in the dark, in the lamp room, and said to the Light: "You are a clever Light. You shine, and you hide, and you shine again, and you save the ships, and you confuse the enemy, and you do it all in three minutes, every hour, which is the most a Light can do, in a war, and it is enough, and it is more than enough, and I am proud of you, Light, as I am proud of my son, and as I was proud of Mary, and as I will always be proud, of this rock, and this Light, and this life."

In 1943, the order changed again. The Light was to be lit, all night, every night, because the war had turned, and the danger had passed, and the ships needed the Light, fully, and Thomas lit it, and it shone, all night, and the ships came, and went, and Thomas's son came home, in 1943, on a ship, guided by the Light, and Thomas, standing on the rock, watching the ship come in, thought: the Light is lit, and my son is home, and the war will end, one day, and the Light will shine, all night, every night, as it always did, and as it always will, because a lighthouse keeper keeps the Light, in the dark, and in the war, and in the peace, and that is his duty, and his life, and his home, and no order can take it away, and no darkness can put it out, not for long, not ever, as long as there is a keeper, on the rock, to light it again.

William came up to the lamp room, that night, and he stood beside his father, and they watched the Light turn, together, father and son, keeper and sailor, and William said, "Father, I looked for the Light, every night, at sea, and when it was dark, I knew why, and I was proud, and when it shone, for three minutes, I fixed my position by it, and I came home by it, and I am home now, because of the Light, and because of you." And Thomas said, "Son, the Light is yours now, too. It has always been yours. You were born in it, in a storm, and you have lived by it, at sea, and one day, when I am gone, you will keep it, or someone will keep it, and the Light will shine, and the ships will come home, and that is the way it is, and the way it will always be, as long as there are rocks, and ships, and men, and lights, to guide them home.

# Demo: The Lighthouse Keeper's War
import re
ABBREV = {"st", "mr", "mrs", "ms", "dr", "jr", "sr", "capt", "lt", "gen", "col", "rev", "hon", "prof", "fig", "no", "vol", "pp", "etc", "vs", "ave", "blvd", "u.s", "e.g", "i.e", "m", "mm", "mme", "fr", "b.c", "a.d"}
def split_sentences(text):
    text = " ".join(text.split())
    bounds = []
    for m in re.finditer(r'[.!?]["\u201d\u2019]?\s+', text):
        before = text[:m.start()].rstrip()
        tok = before.split()[-1].lower().rstrip(".") if before.split() else ""
        if tok in ABBREV:
            continue
        bounds.append(m.end())
    out, start = [], 0
    for b in bounds:
        out.append(text[start:b].strip())
        start = b
    tail = text[start:].strip()
    if tail:
        out.append(tail)
    return [s for s in out if s]

# Program: The Lighthouse Keeper's War
import re
ABBREV = {"st", "mr", "mrs", "ms", "dr", "jr", "sr", "capt", "lt", "gen", "col", "rev", "hon", "prof", "fig", "no", "vol", "pp", "etc", "vs", "ave", "blvd", "u.s", "e.g", "i.e", "m", "mm", "mme", "fr", "b.c", "a.d"}
def split_sentences(text):
    text = " ".join(text.split())
    bounds = []
    for m in re.finditer(r'[.!?]["\u201d\u2019]?\s+', text):
        before = text[:m.start()].rstrip()
        tok = before.split()[-1].lower().rstrip(".") if before.split() else ""
        if tok in ABBREV:
            continue
        bounds.append(m.end())
    out, start = [], 0
    for b in bounds:
        out.append(text[start:b].strip())
        start = b
    tail = text[start:].strip()
    if tail:
        out.append(tail)
    return [s for s in out if s]

Gertrude, a white goat with a brown patch over one eye, is elected mayor of a village of four hundred people by a show of hands on market day, and turns out to be the best mayor the village ever had, because she listens, does not pretend, and eats the foolish proposals. A comedy about local politics, potholes, and a goat.

Full text

My neighbour's goat became the mayor on a Tuesday, which was unfortunate, because Tuesdays are market days, and the market was full, and everyone saw it happen, and no one could pretend, afterwards, that it had not happened, which is the first rule of small-town politics: if it happens on market day, it has happened, and it will be remembered, and it will be talked about, for years.

My neighbour is a man named Mr. Abernathy, although everyone calls him Bert, and Bert keeps a goat, named Gertrude, who is a white goat, with a brown patch over one eye, and a habit of eating things she should not eat, including, on one memorable occasion, the vicar's hat, and on another, the minutes of the parish council meeting, which Bert said was the most useful thing Gertrude had ever eaten, because the minutes were boring, and Gertrude, by eating them, had improved them.

On the Tuesday in question, there was an election. It was not a big election. It was a small election, for the mayor of our village, which is a village of four hundred people, and a goat, and the candidates were two: Mrs. Pemberton, who had been the mayor for twelve years, and who was very good at being the mayor, in the way that people who have been the mayor for twelve years are very good at it, which is to say, she knew everyone's name, and everyone's business, and she ran the meetings on time, and she cut the ribbons, and she opened the fetes; and Mr. Collins, who was a newcomer, who had lived in the village for three years, which, in village terms, made him practically a tourist, and who wanted to be the mayor because he had been the mayor of somewhere else, once, and he missed it, and he thought our village needed "fresh ideas", which is what newcomers always think, and what villagers always dread.

The election was held in the village hall, and the voting was by a show of hands, because that is how we do it, in our village, and the counting was done by Bert, because Bert is the parish clerk, and because Bert is honest, and because Bert, as everyone knows, cannot count past twenty without taking his shoes off, which is why the counting took a long time, and why, in the middle of it, Gertrude got loose.

Gertrude had come with Bert, because Bert takes Gertrude everywhere, and Gertrude was tied up outside the village hall, and she got loose, because Gertrude is very good at getting loose, and she came into the hall, through the back door, which someone had left open, and she walked up to the front, where the counting was happening, and she stood there, looking at the crowd, with her brown patch over one eye, and she ate a piece of paper, which happened to be a ballot paper, and Bert, who was counting, said, "Gertrude, no," and Gertrude, who does not listen, ate another piece of paper, and then she sat down, in the mayor's chair, which was empty, because Mrs. Pemberton was standing, counting, and Mr. Collins was standing, counting, and Gertrude sat in the chair, and she looked at the crowd, and the crowd looked at her, and someone, in the back, said, "Well, she can't do any worse than the last lot," and someone else said, "Hear, hear," and someone else said, "All in favour of the goat?" and before anyone knew what was happening, every hand in the hall went up, except for Mrs. Pemberton's, and Mr. Collins's, and Bert's, because Bert was trying to get Gertrude out of the chair, and Gertrude would not move, because Gertrude, once she has sat down, does not move, until she is ready, and she was not ready.

And so Gertrude became the mayor. Not officially, at first. Officially, Mrs. Pemberton won, by three votes, after the recount, which Bert did twice, once with his shoes on, and once with his shoes off, to be sure. But unofficially, in the way that matters, in a village, Gertrude became the mayor, because the people had voted for her, with their hands, in the hall, on market day, and because Mrs. Pemberton, who was a wise woman, and who knew the village, said, "Very well. If the people want the goat, the people shall have the goat. I will be the deputy mayor. Gertrude will be the mayor. And Bert will be — Bert, you will be the mayor's keeper, and you will bring her to the meetings, and you will translate, because Gertrude does not speak, except in bleats, and bleats, as we all know, are open to interpretation."

And that is how my neighbour's goat became the mayor. She attended the meetings, sitting in the mayor's chair, eating the minutes, when Bert was not looking, and the meetings, which had once been boring, became interesting, because no one knew what Gertrude would do next, and because Gertrude, it turned out, was very good at being the mayor, in the way that goats are very good at things, which is to say, she listened, and she did not interrupt, and she did not pretend to know things she did not know, and when someone proposed something foolish, Gertrude ate the proposal, which was, as Bert said, the most efficient form of veto ever devised.

Bert's job, as the mayor's keeper and translator, was harder than it looked. He had to bring Gertrude to the meetings, on time, which meant coaxing her out of the garden, where she was eating the roses, and he had to sit beside her, and interpret her bleats, for the minutes, and the interpretations were, Bert admitted, largely invented, but they were invented in the spirit of Gertrude, which is to say, sensibly, and with a certain amount of impatience for foolishness. When Gertrude bleated once, Bert wrote: "The Mayor notes the proposal and requests further information." When she bleated twice, he wrote: "The Mayor has reservations." When she ate the proposal, he wrote: "The Mayor has vetoed the proposal, on the grounds that it is, in her words, 'inedible', which the Keeper interprets as 'unacceptable'."

The first great test of Gertrude's mayoralty came in the autumn, when Mr. Hardcastle, who owned the field at the edge of the village, proposed to build six houses on it, without planning permission, without consulting anyone, and with a great deal of confidence, because Mr. Hardcastle was a confident man, and because he thought the village would not object, and because he had not counted on Gertrude. He came to the meeting, with plans, and with a lawyer, and he laid the plans on the table, and Gertrude, who had been dozing, woke up, and she looked at the plans, and she sniffed them, and she ate them, all of them, slowly, and thoroughly, while Mr. Hardcastle watched, and his lawyer watched, and the council watched, and Bert wrote, in the minutes: "The Mayor has considered the planning application, and has eaten it. The application is therefore refused. The Mayor suggests that Mr. Hardcastle plant the field with wildflowers, instead, which the Mayor would enjoy eating, and which would be of benefit to the bees."

Mr. Hardcastle objected. He wrote to the county council. He wrote to his Member of Parliament. He wrote to the newspapers. And the county council sent an inspector, a severe woman named Miss Grimshaw, no relation to the hinge firm, who came to the village, and who demanded to see the mayor, and who was taken to Bert's garden, where Gertrude was eating the grass, and Miss Grimshaw said, "This is the mayor? This is a goat."

"Yes," Bert said. "She is the mayor. She was elected, by a show of hands, on market day, and she has served for a year, and the village is thriving, and the potholes are filled, and the bus shelter is built, and the fete was the best in years, and if you would like to inspect her record, it is in the minutes, although some of the minutes have been eaten, which is, in itself, a record of her decisions."

Miss Grimshaw inspected. She read the minutes. She talked to Mrs. Pemberton. She talked to the vicar, who had lost two hats to Gertrude, and who said, "She is a good mayor. She listens. She does not pretend. And she has never, to my knowledge, told a lie, which is more than can be said for most politicians." Miss Grimshaw went back to the county council, and she wrote a report, which said: "The village of — has a goat for a mayor. This is irregular. This is unprecedented. This is, however, working. The village is well-run, the accounts are in order, and the residents are happy. I recommend that we leave them alone, and that we do not interfere, because interfering with a system that works, in order to replace it with a system that does not, is the definition of bureaucracy, and I did not become an inspector to be a definition."

The county council left them alone. Mr. Hardcastle planted the field with wildflowers, in the end, because he had nothing else to do with it, and because the bees came, and the village liked the bees, and Gertrude liked the wildflowers, and everyone, except Mr. Hardcastle, was happy, and Mr. Hardcastle, in time, became happy too, because he discovered that he liked beekeeping, and that beekeeping was more satisfying than building houses, and he became the village beekeeper, and he kept his bees in the field, and Gertrude ate the wildflowers, carefully, around the hives, and the whole thing worked out, in the way that things work out, in a village, when the mayor is a goat, and the goat eats the foolish proposals, and the people listen, and the bees come, and the wildflowers grow.

The village thrived, under Gertrude. The fete was the best in years, because Gertrude opened it, by eating the ribbon, which was faster than cutting it, and more memorable. The potholes were filled, because Gertrude, walking to the meetings, kept falling into them, and Bert, tired of pulling her out, filled them himself, with gravel, and a shovel, and a great deal of muttering. The parish council, which had argued for years about the new bus shelter, agreed, unanimously, to build it, because Gertrude, on a rainy day, had stood under the old shelter, and it had leaked on her, and Bert had said, "Look. The mayor is wet. Are we going to let the mayor be wet?" and the council had said no, they were not, and the shelter was built, within a month, which was the fastest the council had ever done anything, in living memory.

Mr. Collins left the village, after a year, because he said the village had "lost its way", and because he missed being the mayor of somewhere else, and Mrs. Pemberton, who was the deputy mayor, and who did most of the work, said, "Gertrude is the best mayor we have ever had, because she does not want to be the mayor, and she does not pretend to be anything she is not, and she eats the foolish proposals, and she listens, and she is, in her way, honest, which is more than can be said for most mayors, in most places, in most times."

Gertrude was the mayor for six years. She retired, in the end, because she got old, and because her legs got stiff, and because Bert said it was time, and the village held a retirement party, in the village hall, and everyone came, and Gertrude sat in the mayor's chair, one last time, and she ate the minutes, one last time, and Bert, who was crying, a little, said, "Gertrude, you were the best mayor this village ever had, and I am proud of you, and I am proud to be your keeper, and your neighbour, and your friend." And Gertrude, who does not speak, except in bleats, bleated, once, softly, and everyone, in the hall, understood, in the way that people in a village understand a goat, that she was saying: thank you, and I loved it, and I would do it again, if I could, but I am old, and tired, and it is time for someone else, and whoever it is, I hope they eat the foolish proposals, and listen, and do not pretend, and that is all any mayor can do, goat or human, in any village, in any time.

Mrs. Pemberton became the mayor again, after Gertrude, and she was very good at it, as she had always been, and Bert became the deputy mayor, and Gertrude lived out her days, in Bert's garden, eating the grass, and the flowers, and, occasionally, the vicar's hat, when the vicar was not looking, and the village remembered her, and the story was told, on market days, and at fetes, and in the pub, and it was told, and retold, until it became a legend, and the legend was this: once, in our village, the mayor was a goat, and she was the best mayor we ever had, because she listened, and she did not pretend, and she ate the foolish proposals, and that, in the end, is what a mayor is for.

The neighbouring village, hearing of Gertrude, decided to try it themselves, and they elected a cat, named Chairman Meow, who was a handsome cat, and who sat in the mayor's chair, and who slept through the meetings, and who ate nothing, except the occasional sandwich, left unattended, and the neighbouring village, after a year, gave up, and went back to a human mayor, and they said, "It is not the animal that matters. It is the goat. It is Gertrude. There will never be another Gertrude, and we were foolish to think that any animal would do, because Gertrude was not just any animal, she was a mayor, and a mayor, goat or human, is a rare thing, and must be recognised, when it appears, and honoured, when it retires, and remembered, when it is gone." And our village, hearing this, nodded, wisely, and said, "Quite right. There will never be another Gertrude," and they put up a plaque, in the village hall, beside the mayor's chair, which said: "GERTRUDE, MAYOR, 6 YEARS. SHE LISTENED. SHE DID NOT PRETEND. SHE ATE THE FOOLISH PROPOSALS." And the plaque is still there, and the chair is still there, and the minutes, some of them eaten, are still in the parish records, with Bert's careful handwriting, and his translations, and his note, in the margin, on the last page: "The Mayor has retired. The village is grateful. The goat was the best of us." And Bert, who still keeps goats, and who still tells the story, on market days, always ends it the same way: "She was a goat. She was the mayor. And she was the best of us. All of us.

And Bert will be — Bert, you will be the mayor\'s keeper, and you will bring her to the meetings, and you will translate, because Gertrude does not speak, except in bleats, and bleats, as we all know, are open to interpretation."\n\nAnd that is how my neighbour\'s goat became the mayor. She attended the meetings, sitting in the mayor\'s chair, eating the minutes, when Bert was not looking, and the meetings, which had once been boring, became interesting, because no one knew what Gertrude would do next, and because Gertrude, it turned out, was very good at being the mayor, in the way that goats are very good at things, which is to say, she listened, and she did not interrupt, and she did not pretend to know things she did not know, and when someone proposed something foolish, Gertrude ate the proposal, which was, as Bert said, the most efficient form of veto ever devised.\n\nBert\'s job, as the mayor\'s keeper and translator, was harder than it looked. He had to bring Gertrude to the meetings, on time, which meant coaxing her out of the garden, where she was eating the roses, and he had to sit beside her, and interpret her bleats, for the minutes, and the interpretations were, Bert admitted, largely invented, but they were invented in the spirit of Gertrude, which is to say, sensibly, and with a certain amount of impatience for foolishness. When Gertrude bleated once, Bert wrote: "The Mayor notes the proposal and requests further information." When she bleated twice, he wrote: "The Mayor has reservations." When she ate the proposal, he wrote: "The Mayor has vetoed the proposal, on the grounds that it is, in her words, \'inedible\', which the Keeper interprets as \'unacceptable\'."\n\nThe first great test of Gertrude\'s mayoralty came in the autumn, when Mr. Hardcastle, who owned the field at the edge of the village, proposed to build six houses on it, without planning permission, without consulting anyone, and with a great deal of confidence, because Mr. Hardcastle was a confident man, and because he thought the village would not object, and because he had not counted on Gertrude. He came to the meeting, with plans, and with a lawyer, and he laid the plans on the table, and Gertrude, who had been dozing, woke up, and she looked at the plans, and she sniffed them, and she ate them, all of them, slowly, and thoroughly, while Mr. Hardcastle watched, and his lawyer watched, and the council watched, and Bert wrote, in the minutes: "The Mayor has considered the planning application, and has eaten it. The application is therefore refused. The Mayor suggests that Mr. Hardcastle plant the field with wildflowers, instead, which the Mayor would enjoy eating, and which would be of benefit to the bees."\n\nMr. Hardcastle objected. He wrote to the county council. He wrote to his Member of Parliament. He wrote to the newspapers. And the county council sent an inspector, a severe woman named Miss Grimshaw, no relation to the hinge firm, who came to the village, and who demanded to see the mayor, and who was taken to Bert\'s garden, where Gertrude was eating the grass, and Miss Grimshaw said, "This is the mayor? This is a goat."\n\n"Yes," Bert said. "She is the mayor. She was elected, by a show of hands, on market day, and she has served for a year, and the village is thriving, and the potholes are filled, and the bus shelter is built, and the fete was the best in years, and if you would like to inspect her record, it is in the minutes, although some of the minutes have been eaten, which is, in itself, a record of her decisions."\n\nMiss Grimshaw inspected. She read the minutes. She talked to Mrs. Pemberton. She talked to the vicar, who had lost two hats to Gertrude, and who said, "She is a good mayor. She listens. She does not pretend. And she has never, to my knowledge, told a lie, which is more than can be said for most politicians." Miss Grimshaw went back to the county council, and she wrote a report, which said: "The village of — has a goat for a mayor. This is irregular. This is unprecedented. This is, however, working. The village is well-run, the accounts are in order, and the residents are happy. I recommend that we leave them alone, and that we do not interfere, because interfering with a system that works, in order to replace it with a system that does not, is the definition of bureaucracy, and I did not become an inspector to be a definition."\n\nThe county council left them alone. Mr. Hardcastle planted the field with wildflowers, in the end, because he had nothing else to do with it, and because the bees came, and the village liked the bees, and Gertrude liked the wildflowers, and everyone, except Mr. Hardcastle, was happy, and Mr. Hardcastle, in time, became happy too, because he discovered that he liked beekeeping, and that beekeeping was more satisfying than building houses, and he became the village beekeeper, and he kept his bees in the field, and Gertrude ate the wildflowers, carefully, around the hives, and the whole thing worked out, in the way that things work out, in a village, when the mayor is a goat, and the goat eats the foolish proposals, and the people listen, and the bees come, and the wildflowers grow.\n\nThe village thrived, under Gertrude. The fete was the best in years, because Gertrude opened it, by eating the ribbon, which was faster than cutting it, and more memorable. The potholes were filled, because Gertrude, walking to the meetings, kept falling into them, and Bert, tired of pulling her out, filled them himself, with gravel, and a shovel, and a great deal of muttering. The parish council, which had argued for years about the new bus shelter, agreed, unanimously, to build it, because Gertrude, on a rainy day, had stood under the old shelter, and it had leaked on her, and Bert had said, "Look. The mayor is wet. Are we going to let the mayor be wet?" and the council had said no, they were not, and the shelter was built, within a month, which was the fastest the council had ever done anything, in living memory.\n\nMr. Collins left the village, after a year, because he said the village had "lost its way", and because he missed being the mayor of somewhere else, and Mrs. Pemberton, who was the deputy mayor, and who did most of the work, said, "Gertrude is the best mayor we have ever had, because she does not want to be the mayor, and she does not pretend to be anything she is not, and she eats the foolish proposals, and she listens, and she is, in her way, honest, which is more than can be said for most mayors, in most places, in most times."\n\nGertrude was the mayor for six years. She retired, in the end, because she got old, and because her legs got stiff, and because Bert said it was time, and the village held a retirement party, in the village hall, and everyone came, and Gertrude sat in the mayor\'s chair, one last time, and she ate the minutes, one last time, and Bert, who was crying, a little, said, "Gertrude, you were the best mayor this village ever had, and I am proud of you, and I am proud to be your keeper, and your neighbour, and your friend." And Gertrude, who does not speak, except in bleats, bleated, once, softly, and everyone, in the hall, understood, in the way that people in a village understand a goat, that she was saying: thank you, and I loved it, and I would do it again, if I could, but I am old, and tired, and it is time for someone else, and whoever it is, I hope they eat the foolish proposals, and listen, and do not pretend, and that is all any mayor can do, goat or human, in any village, in any time.\n\nMrs. Pemberton became the mayor again, after Gertrude, and she was very good at it, as she had always been, and Bert became the deputy mayor, and Gertrude lived out her days, in Bert\'s garden, eating the grass, and the flowers, and, occasionally, the vicar\'s hat, when the vicar was not looking, and the village remembered her, and the story was told, on market days, and at fetes, and in the pub, and it was told, and retold, until it became a legend, and the legend was this: once, in our village, the mayor was a goat, and she was the best mayor we ever had, because she listened, and she did not pretend, and she ate the foolish proposals, and that, in the end, is what a mayor is for.\n\nThe neighbouring village, hearing of Gertrude, decided to try it themselves, and they elected a cat, named Chairman Meow, who was a handsome cat, and who sat in the mayor\'s chair, and who slept through the meetings, and who ate nothing, except the occasional sandwich, left unattended, and the neighbouring village, after a year, gave up, and went back to a human mayor, and they said, "It is not the animal that matters. It is the goat. It is Gertrude. There will never be another Gertrude, and we were foolish to think that any animal would do, because Gertrude was not just any animal, she was a mayor, and a mayor, goat or human, is a rare thing, and must be recognised, when it appears, and honoured, when it retires, and remembered, when it is gone." And our village, hearing this, nodded, wisely, and said, "Quite right. There will never be another Gertrude," and they put up a plaque, in the village hall, beside the mayor\'s chair, which said: "GERTRUDE, MAYOR, 6 YEARS. SHE LISTENED. SHE DID NOT PRETEND. SHE ATE THE FOOLISH PROPOSALS." And the plaque is still there, and the chair is still there, and the minutes, some of them eaten, are still in the parish records, with Bert\'s careful handwriting, and his translations, and his note, in the margin, on the last page: "The Mayor has retired. The village is grateful. The goat was the best of us." And Bert, who still keeps goats, and who still tells the story, on market days, always ends it the same way: "She was a goat. She was the mayor. And she was the best of us. All of us.'

Dr. Amara Chen has counted stars alone on the far side of the Moon for eleven years, four million of them, when a ship lands and a visitor steps out who counts worlds. Together they count stars and worlds, and Amara learns she was never counting alone. A story about loneliness, counting, and first contact.

Full text

On the far side of the Moon, where the Earth never rises, and the sky is black, even at noon, and the silence is so complete that you can hear your own heart beating, in your suit, there lived a woman who counted stars.

Her name was Dr. Amara Chen, and she was fifty-one years old, and she had been on the Moon for eleven years, alone, in a station built for six, because the others had left, one by one, when the funding ran out, and when the missions were cancelled, and when the world, on Earth, had decided that the Moon was not worth the trouble, and Amara had stayed, because someone had to stay, and because the stars needed counting, and because she was the one who counted them.

The station was called Farside, and it was a cluster of domes, and dishes, and solar panels, on the grey dust, under the black sky, and Amara lived in it, alone, with a telescope, and a computer, and a garden, small, green, in a dome, where she grew tomatoes, and lettuce, and herbs, because a person, even on the Moon, needs green things, and needs to watch something grow, in a place where nothing grows, naturally, and never has.

Amara counted stars. She counted them the way other people count sheep, or count money, or count the days until they go home, which is to say, carefully, and patiently, and with a kind of love, because the stars, Amara believed, were not just lights, in the sky, but stories, and each one had a story, and her job, as she saw it, was to count them, and to know their stories, and to keep the count, so that no star was forgotten, and no story was lost.

Amara had come to the Moon eleven years ago, as part of a crew of six, on a mission that was supposed to last two years, and to build a telescope, on the far side, where the sky was darkest, and the stars were clearest, and the crew had built it, and they had counted stars, together, and they had laughed, and argued, and grown tomatoes, in the dome, and then, one by one, they had left. First, Marcus, the engineer, who went home when his wife had a child, and who wrote, afterwards, that he missed the stars, but that he missed his daughter more. Then, Elena, the doctor, who went home when the funding was cut, and the mission was shortened, and who said, as she left: "Amara, you do not have to stay. You can come home. The Moon will still be here." Then, the others, one by one, until Amara was alone, in a station built for six, with a telescope, and a computer, and a garden, and four million stars, and she had stayed, because someone had to stay, and because the stars needed counting, and because she was the one who counted them, and because going home, to a world that had decided the Moon was not worth the trouble, felt like giving up, and Amara did not give up, not on the stars, not on the count, not ever.

Her days had a rhythm, in the station, alone. She woke, at six, station time, and she checked the telescope, and the computer, and the garden, and she ate breakfast, tomatoes, and lettuce, from the dome, and bread, from the stores, which were running low, but which would last, she calculated, for another three years, if she was careful, and she was careful, because Amara was always careful, with numbers, and with food, and with time. She counted stars, in the morning, for four hours, and she ate lunch, and she counted stars, in the afternoon, for four hours, and she tended the garden, and she exercised, on the treadmill, and she wrote in her notebook, and she looked at the sky, through the dome, black, and full of stars, and she thought: this is my life. A station, on the Moon, and a telescope, and a garden, and four million stars, and a count, that grows, every day, by a few more, and that will go on growing, as long as I am here, and I am here, and I will be here, until the count is done, or until I am done, whichever comes first.

Earth had gone silent, three years ago. The link had crackled, and faded, and stopped, and Amara had tried, for a month, to re-establish it, and she had failed, and she had decided, in the end, that Earth had not abandoned her, but had forgotten her, which is a different thing, and a sadder thing, and she had kept counting, because counting was what she did, and because the stars did not forget her, and because the stars, unlike Earth, were always there, in the black sky, waiting to be counted, and Amara counted them, and she kept the count, in the notebook, and in the computer, and she thought, sometimes, about the people on Earth, and about whether they remembered her, and she hoped they did, and she feared they did not, and she counted, anyway, because counting is what you do, when you are alone, and far from home, and the only thing you have is the sky, and the stars, and the count, and the hope that someone, somewhere, is counting too.

She had counted, in eleven years, four million, two hundred and eighteen thousand, six hundred and forty-one stars. She knew the number exactly, because she kept it, in a notebook, and in the computer, and she updated it, every day, and the number grew, slowly, as she found new stars, faint ones, far ones, stars that no one had counted before, because no one had looked, in that part of the sky, with a telescope, on the far side of the Moon, where there was no Earthlight, and no atmosphere, and no noise, only the black sky, and the stars, going on forever.

On the morning of the fourteenth of November, Amara found a star that should not have been there. It was in a part of the sky she had counted, a hundred times, and it was new, and it was bright, and it was moving, slowly, across the sky, in a way that stars do not move, and Amara, who was a practical woman, and who did not believe in miracles, checked her telescope, and her computer, and her notebook, and she found that the star was not a star, but a ship, and the ship was coming toward the Moon, and it was not a human ship, because no human ship had come to the Moon in eleven years, and because the ship was not shaped like any ship Amara had ever seen, and because it was lit, in a way that ships are not lit, with a light that was soft, and blue, and which pulsed, slowly, like a heartbeat.

Amara watched the ship. She watched it for three days, as it came closer, and she did not call Earth, because Earth had not answered her calls in three years, and because the link was dead, and because she was alone, on the far side of the Moon, and the only person she could tell was herself, and herself, she told, in the notebook, in careful handwriting: "A ship is coming. It is not ours. It is lit blue. It pulses. I am not afraid. I am curious. I have counted four million stars, and I have never counted a ship, and now I will count this one, too, and I will learn its story, as I have learned the stories of the stars."

On the fourth day, the ship landed. It landed, gently, in the dust, a kilometre from the station, and it opened, and a figure came out, and the figure was tall, and thin, and it glowed, faintly, blue, and it walked toward the station, slowly, and Amara, who had been alone for eleven years, put on her suit, and went out to meet it, because a person, even on the Moon, even after eleven years alone, does not hide, when a visitor comes, but goes out, and says hello, and asks who they are, and where they have come from, and what they want.

"Hello," Amara said, over the radio, in her suit. "I am Dr. Amara Chen. I count stars. Who are you?"

The figure stopped. It looked at her. It said, in a voice that came through her radio, clear, and calm: "I am a counter, too. I count worlds. I have counted four thousand, two hundred and eighteen worlds, and I have come to count yours, and to learn its story, and to keep the count, so that no world is forgotten, and no story is lost."

Amara laughed. She had not laughed in a long time, and the laugh surprised her, and the figure, which glowed blue, tilted its head, and said, "Why do you laugh?"

"Because," Amara said, "I have counted four million stars, and you have counted four thousand worlds, and we are both counters, and we have both come to the same place, on the far side of the Moon, to count, and to learn, and I think that is the most wonderful thing I have ever heard, and I think we should count together."

And so they did. Amara and the counter, who called itself Lyra, counted together, for a year, and then for another year, and Amara showed Lyra the stars, and Lyra showed Amara the worlds, and they counted the stars, and the worlds, and they kept the count, in the notebook, and in the computer, and in Lyra's memory, which was larger than any computer, and they learned each other's stories, and they became friends, in the way that counters become friends, which is to say, slowly, and patiently, and by counting, together, in the dark, under the black sky, on the far side of the Moon, where the Earth never rises, and where the silence is so complete that you can hear your own heart beating, and the heart of a friend, beating beside you, in a suit, in the dust, under the stars.

Lyra told Amara about the worlds it had counted. There was a world of water, where the people lived on boats, and never saw land, and counted the waves, the way Amara counted stars. There was a world of ice, where the people lived under the ice, and counted the days until the thaw, which never came, and counted them anyway, because counting is hope, and hope is what you do, when the thaw never comes. There was a world of light, where the sun never set, and the people counted the shadows, which were rare, and precious, and which they kept, in boxes, and showed to their children, as treasures. And there was a world, Lyra said, that was like Earth, but not Earth, where the people had counted stars, too, and had built a station, on their moon, and had stayed, alone, counting, and Lyra had visited them, and had counted with them, and had left, and had thought of them, often, and had wondered if they were still counting, and if they were still alone, and if they would like to know that they were not alone, and that there were other counters, in the dark, counting too.

Amara told Lyra about the stars. She told it about the star that was the first she had ever counted, when she was a child, on Earth, looking up, with her father, who had pointed, and said, "That one, Amara. That one is yours. Count it, and remember it, and it will always be yours, no matter where you go." She told it about the star that pulsed, and the star that flared, and the star that had died, a million years ago, and whose light was still travelling, and would arrive, one day, and would be counted, by someone, somewhere, who did not know it was dead, and who would count it anyway, because counting a dead star is still counting, and still matters. She told it about the four million stars, and about the notebook, and about the number, four million, two hundred and eighteen thousand, six hundred and forty-one, and about how the number grew, every day, and about how, one day, the number would be five million, and then six, and then more, and about how the count would never be done, because the stars go on forever, and counting them is a life's work, and a life's work is never done, only continued, by someone, somewhere, who picks up the count, and carries it on.

Lyra listened. It listened, in the way that counters listen, which is completely, and without interrupting, and it said, "Amara. I have counted four thousand worlds, and I have met many counters, and you are the best counter I have ever met, because you count not only the stars, but the stories, and the stories are what matter, and the count is only the way you keep them, and I am glad I came to your Moon, and I am glad I found you, alone, counting, and I will remember you, and your stars, and your count, for as long as I count, which will be for a very long time, and perhaps forever."

In the end, Lyra left. It had counted the Moon, and the Earth, and the stars, and it had learned their stories, and it had to go, to count other worlds, in other places, and Amara, standing in the dust, watching the ship go, blue, and pulsing, into the black sky, thought: I have counted four million stars, and I have counted one friend, and the friend is the best thing I have ever counted, and the stars are still there, and I am still here, and the count goes on, and it will go on, as long as there is someone, on the far side of the Moon, to count, and to keep the count, and to tell the stories, so that no star is forgotten, and no world is forgotten, and no friend is forgotten, ever.

Before it left, Lyra gave Amara a gift. It was a map, not of the Moon, or of the Earth, but of the stars, as Lyra saw them, from its worlds, and the map showed the same stars, from a different side, and Amara looked at it, and she understood, suddenly, that the stars are the same, everywhere, and that counting them, from the Moon, or from a world of water, or a world of ice, is the same work, and that the counters, everywhere, are doing the same work, and that they are, all of them, together, in the dark, counting, and keeping the count, and telling the stories, so that nothing is forgotten. Lyra said, "Keep this map, Amara. And when you count, remember that I am counting too, somewhere, and that the count is shared, and that you are not alone, even on the far side of the Moon, even when Earth is silent, even when the station is empty, because the counters are everywhere, and we are all counting together, one star at a time, one world at a time, for as long as it takes, and for as long as there are stars to count, and worlds to count, and stories to tell.

# Demo: The Woman Who Counted Stars
import re
ABBREV = {"st", "mr", "mrs", "ms", "dr", "jr", "sr", "capt", "lt", "gen", "col", "rev", "hon", "prof", "fig", "no", "vol", "pp", "etc", "vs", "ave", "blvd", "u.s", "e.g", "i.e", "m", "mm", "mme", "fr", "b.c", "a.d"}
def split_sentences(text):
    text = " ".join(text.split())
    bounds = []
    for m in re.finditer(r'[.!?]["\u201d\u2019]?\s+', text):
        before = text[:m.start()].rstrip()
        tok = before.split()[-1].lower().rstrip(".") if before.split() else ""
        if tok in ABBREV:
            continue
        bounds.append(m.end())
    out, start = [], 0
    for b in bounds:
        out.append(text[start:b].strip())
        start = b
    tail = text[start:].strip()
    if tail:
        out.append(tail)
    return [s for s in out if s]

# Program: The Woman Who Counted Stars
import re
ABBREV = {"st", "mr", "mrs", "ms", "dr", "jr", "sr", "capt", "lt", "gen", "col", "rev", "hon", "prof", "fig", "no", "vol", "pp", "etc", "vs", "ave", "blvd", "u.s", "e.g", "i.e", "m", "mm", "mme", "fr", "b.c", "a.d"}
def split_sentences(text):
    text = " ".join(text.split())
    bounds = []
    for m in re.finditer(r'[.!?]["\u201d\u2019]?\s+', text):
        before = text[:m.start()].rstrip()
        tok = before.split()[-1].lower().rstrip(".") if before.split() else ""
        if tok in ABBREV:
            continue
        bounds.append(m.end())
    out, start = [], 0
    for b in bounds:
        out.append(text[start:b].strip())
        start = b
    tail = text[start:].strip()
    if tail:
        out.append(tail)
    return [s for s in out if s]

Miriam and her eight-year-old daughter Lucy move into the house on the bend, empty for eleven years, where footsteps walk the stairs at night and a voice asks for letters hidden behind the fireplace. The letters explain why the Harrow family fled, and finding them sets the house free. A story about haunted houses, and the ones that are only sad.

An original Signature short story in the literary genre, written for The Publishable Short Stories Database (Signature Edition) in 2026. It was created as a complete publishable work, with no prior publication and no model on any existing story.

The haunting is a filing problem: the footsteps are a message that cannot be delivered until someone finds the letters, and once they are found the house goes quiet. The story opens with: “The house on the bend had been empty for eleven years, and everyone in the village knew why, and no one talked about it, except in whispers, on winter evenings, when the wind came down from the hill, and the house, on the bend, creaked, in a way that houses should not creak, unless someone is in them, walking, and there was no one in it, because it had been empty for eleven years.” and closes with: “And the footsteps, which had walked the stairs for eleven years, walked no more, because the letters had been found, and the house, at last, could rest.” Across 19 paragraphs and 82 sentences, the opening promise and the closing line frame the whole arc, and the ending re-reads the beginning: what the first sentence sets in motion, the last sentence settles.
