Full text

The audition was for a play, and the play was a tragedy, and the tragedy was that no one who auditioned could act, including, and especially, the director, who was a man named Mr. Pemberton, who had directed twelve plays, and who had learned nothing from any of them, except that auditions are the worst part of directing, because auditions are where you discover that the people who want to be in your play cannot act, and that the people who can act do not want to be in your play, because they have seen your last play, and they have decided, wisely, to stay away.

Mr. Pemberton had put up a notice, in the village hall, and in the shop, and in the pub, and it said: "AUDITIONS FOR 'THE TRAGEDY OF KING LEAR' — ALL WELCOME — NO EXPERIENCE NECESSARY — BRING YOUR OWN CROWN (IF YOU HAVE ONE)". He had chosen King Lear, because it was a great play, and because he had always wanted to direct it, and because he had forgotten, or had never known, that King Lear has a cast of twenty, and that our village has a population of four hundred, of whom perhaps ten can act, and of whom perhaps two are willing to admit it, in public, on a Tuesday evening, in the village hall, in front of Mr. Pemberton, who was, as everyone knew, a difficult man, to audition for, because he shouted, and because he wept, at the auditions, when the acting was bad, and the acting was always bad, and so Mr. Pemberton wept, a great deal, at auditions.

On the Tuesday evening, seven people came. There was Mrs. Abernathy, who was sixty-eight, and who wanted to play Lear, because she had played Lear, once, in 1974, in a different village, and she had been magnificent, or so she said, and no one had been there to contradict her, because it was 1974, and a different village, and Mrs. Abernathy's memory of 1974 was, by her own admission, "selective, but vivid". There was Bert, from the shop, who wanted to play the Fool, because he was, in his own words, "a natural fool", and because he had a hat, with bells on it, which he had bought, especially, for the audition, and which he wore, to the audition, and which jingled, when he walked, and which Mr. Pemberton said was "distracting, but committed". There was Sanjay, from the post office, who wanted to play Edmund, because Edmund was a villain, and Sanjay had always wanted to play a villain, because villains, Sanjay believed, had the best lines, and the best costumes, and did not have to be likeable, which suited Sanjay, who was likeable, but who was tired of being likeable, and who wanted, for once, to be unlikeable, on stage, in front of people, and to enjoy it.

There was a young woman named Poppy, who was nineteen, and who wanted to play Cordelia, because Cordelia was the good daughter, and Poppy was a good daughter, and because she had a clear voice, and because she had learned the lines, all of them, and she said them, at the audition, clearly, and beautifully, and Mr. Pemberton wept, not because the acting was bad, but because it was good, and because good acting, at an audition, is rarer than bad acting, and more moving, and Mr. Pemberton, who wept at bad acting, wept more at good acting, because good acting reminded him of what the play could be, and what it probably would not be, given the other six people in the room.

There was a man named Gerald, who was seventy-five, and who wanted to play Gloucester, because Gloucester loses his eyes, in the play, and Gerald, who had lost his glasses, three times, in the last week, felt a kinship with Gloucester, and because he had a beard, which he believed was "very Gloucester", and which Mr. Pemberton said was "very beard", and which was, in the end, the same thing, as far as Gerald was concerned.

There was a woman named Fiona, who was forty-two, and who wanted to play Regan, because Regan was a villain, and Fiona, who was a solicitor, and who was used to being disliked, professionally, wanted to be disliked, theatrically, as well, and because she had a laugh, which she described as "a Regan laugh", and which she demonstrated, at the audition, and which made everyone in the room, including Mr. Pemberton, take a step backwards, which Fiona took as a compliment, and which it was, in a way.

And there was me. I wanted to play the King of France, because the King of France has very few lines, and because he marries Cordelia, and because Poppy was playing Cordelia, and because I had admired Poppy, from a distance, for a year, and because the King of France, in the play, is the only man who sees Cordelia's worth, when no one else does, and I thought, if I played him, Poppy might see my worth, too, which was a foolish reason to audition for a play, but it was my reason, and it was honest, and honesty, in auditions, is rarer than talent, and more valuable, in the end.

Mr. Pemberton auditioned us, one by one. Mrs. Abernathy played Lear, and she was magnificent, in the way that a woman of sixty-eight, playing an eighty-year-old king, in a village hall, on a Tuesday evening, can be magnificent, which is to say, loudly, and with great conviction, and with a crown made of cardboard, which she had brought, herself, because the notice had said to bring your own crown, if you have one, and Mrs. Abernathy had one, because she had kept it, from 1974, in a different village, where she had been magnificent, and where no one had contradicted her.

Bert played the Fool, with his hat, with bells, and he jingled, and he joked, and he was, as he had said, a natural fool, and Mr. Pemberton said, "Bert, you are not acting. You are simply being yourself, with bells on." And Bert said, "Is that not what acting is, Mr. Pemberton? Being yourself, with bells on?" And Mr. Pemberton, who had directed twelve plays, and who had learned nothing from any of them, said, "Bert, you may have a point. You are the Fool."

Sanjay played Edmund, and he was a villain, and he enjoyed it, and he said his lines, with a snarl, and Mr. Pemberton said, "Sanjay, you are too likeable, to be a villain," and Sanjay said, "That is the point, Mr. Pemberton. The best villains are likeable. That is why they are dangerous." And Mr. Pemberton, who had never thought of it that way, said, "Sanjay, you are Edmund."

Poppy played Cordelia, and she was beautiful, and clear, and Mr. Pemberton wept, and said, "Poppy, you are Cordelia. You have always been Cordelia. You were born to be Cordelia, and I am only sorry it took me twelve plays to find you."

Gerald played Gloucester, and he lost his glasses, in the middle of his speech, and he carried on, without them, and Mr. Pemberton said, "Gerald, that was the most Gloucester thing I have ever seen. You are Gloucester."

Fiona played Regan, and she laughed, her Regan laugh, and everyone took a step backwards, and Mr. Pemberton said, "Fiona, you are Regan. You are terrifying. Please, never laugh like that, except on stage, and preferably, not at me."

And I played the King of France. I said my lines, all four of them, clearly, and I looked at Poppy, as Cordelia, and I said, "She is herself a dowry," which is what the King of France says, about Cordelia, and Poppy looked at me, and she smiled, a little, and Mr. Pemberton said, "You. You are the King of France. You have four lines, and you said them well, and you looked at Cordelia, as if you meant them, and that is more than most Kings of France do, in most productions, in most villages, in most times."

And so we were cast. Mrs. Abernathy as Lear. Bert as the Fool. Sanjay as Edmund. Poppy as Cordelia. Gerald as Gloucester. Fiona as Regan. And me, as the King of France. And Mr. Pemberton, who had directed twelve plays, and who had learned nothing from any of them, looked at us, seven people, in a village hall, on a Tuesday evening, and he wept, and he said, "This. This is a cast. This is a play. This is King Lear. And we will be magnificent. Or we will be terrible. But we will be together, and we will do it, and that is what theatre is, in the end: seven people, in a village hall, who cannot act, except for one, who can, and who will carry us all, and we will be grateful, and we will try, and trying, in theatre, is everything."

We rehearsed, for three months. We learned our lines. We built a set, out of cardboard, and paint, and hope. Mrs. Abernathy wore her crown, from 1974. Bert wore his hat, with bells. Sanjay snarled. Poppy was beautiful. Gerald lost his glasses, twice a rehearsal. Fiona laughed, and everyone stepped backwards. And I, the King of France, said my four lines, and looked at Poppy, and Poppy smiled, a little, and then a little more, and then, one evening, after rehearsal, she said, "You are a good King of France," and I said, "Thank you. You are a good Cordelia," and she said, "Would you like to have tea, sometime? Not as the King of France. As yourself." And I said yes, and we had tea, and then we had tea again, and then we were not just the King of France, and Cordelia, but ourselves, and ourselves, it turned out, liked each other, very much, which was a better ending, than any in King Lear, which, as everyone knows, ends badly, for almost everyone, except the King of France, who leaves, early, with Cordelia, and who, in our production, left, early, with Cordelia, and lived happily ever after, or at least, happily, for now, which is the best any of us can hope for, in theatre, or in life, or in a village hall, on a Tuesday evening, in front of Mr. Pemberton, who wept, when he saw us, together, and who said, "That. That is acting. That is real. And that is why we do it, all of us, even when we cannot act, especially when we cannot act, because sometimes, in trying, we find something real, and something true, and something that lasts, longer than the play, and longer than the applause, and that is the audition, and the rehearsal, and the performance, all in one, and it is enough."

The rehearsals were a disaster, in the best possible way. In the first week, Mrs. Abernathy's crown, from 1974, broke, in the middle of the storm scene, and the cardboard fell, in pieces, onto the stage, and Mrs. Abernathy, without missing a beat, picked up a piece, and held it, like a sceptre, and said, "Blow, winds, and crack your cheeks!" and Mr. Pemberton, who had been about to weep, laughed, instead, and said, "Mrs. Abernathy, that was magnificent. Keep the broken crown. It is better broken. Lear is broken. The crown should be broken, too." In the second week, Gerald lost his glasses, on stage, during the blinding scene, which was, Mr. Pemberton said, "method acting, of the highest order, although unintentional, and although Gerald could not see, which made it, in a way, more authentic, because Gloucester, after all, cannot see either." In the third week, Bert's hat, with bells, lost a bell, which rolled, across the stage, during the most solemn moment in the play, and Bert, chasing it, on all fours, in the middle of a tragedy, made the entire cast laugh, and Mr. Pemberton, wiping his eyes, said, "Bert, you are the Fool. The Fool chases bells. It is in the text. Somewhere. Probably. Keep chasing the bell, Bert. It is the truest thing in this play."

The dress rehearsal was the worst, and the best. The set fell down, twice. The lights went out, once. Fiona's Regan laugh made a child in the audience cry, although there was no audience, only Mr. Pemberton, and the child was Mr. Pemberton's grandson, who had come to watch, and who cried, and Fiona apologised, and the grandson said, "It is all right. She is scary. That is good. Villains should be scary." And Poppy, as Cordelia, forgot a line, and I, as the King of France, prompted her, gently, and she remembered, and she smiled at me, and Mr. Pemberton, watching, said, "That. That is what theatre is. Not the lines, perfectly said, but the lines, remembered, together, and the smile, and the helping, and the being there, for each other, on stage, in the dark, when the set falls down, and the lights go out, and the bell rolls away, and the crown breaks, and still, we go on, because the play must go on, and because we are together, and because that is enough."

On the night of the performance, the village hall was full. Four hundred people, in a hall built for two hundred, sitting on chairs, and on the floor, and standing, at the back, and Mr. Pemberton, backstage, wept, as he always did, and said, "This is it. This is the night. Be magnificent. Or be terrible. But be together." The curtain — which was not a curtain, but a bedsheet, hung on a rope — went up, and Mrs. Abernathy, as Lear, in her broken crown, came on, and she was magnificent, loudly, and with great conviction, and the audience, which had come expecting to be polite, was silent, and then it laughed, in the right places, and it gasped, in the right places, and it cried, in the right places, and Bert, as the Fool, jingled, and joked, and the audience loved him, and Sanjay, as Edmund, snarled, and the audience hated him, which was the point, and Poppy, as Cordelia, was beautiful, and clear, and the audience held its breath, and Gerald, as Gloucester, lost his glasses, on stage, in front of four hundred people, and carried on, without them, and the audience, which knew about Gerald's glasses, applauded, and Fiona, as Regan, laughed, her Regan laugh, and the audience, all four hundred of them, took a step backwards, together, in their seats, which was a remarkable thing to see, and which Fiona took as the greatest compliment of her life.

And I, the King of France, said my four lines, and I looked at Poppy, and Poppy looked at me, and the audience, which knew, by then, about the King of France, and Cordelia, and about the tea, and about ourselves, applauded, louder than for any other moment in the play, because the audience, in a village, knows when something is real, and when something is acted, and the King of France, and Cordelia, were real, and the audience knew it, and they applauded, for us, and for the play, and for Mrs. Abernathy, and Bert, and Sanjay, and Gerald, and Fiona, and Mr. Pemberton, who wept, in the wings, and who came on, at the end, for the curtain call, and who said, to the audience: "Thank you. Thank you for coming. Thank you for laughing, and for gasping, and for crying, and for stepping backwards, together, when Regan laughed. This play was a tragedy, and it was a comedy, and it was a disaster, and it was magnificent, and it was ours, and we did it, together, seven people, in a village hall, who cannot act, except for one, who can, and who carried us all, and I am proud, and I am grateful, and I will direct another play, next year, and I hope you will all audition, again, and bring your own crowns, if you have them, and your own hats, with bells, and your own Regan laughs, and we will do it again, because that is what theatre is, in a village, and in the world: people, together, trying, and failing, and trying again, and finding, in the trying, something real, and something true, and something that lasts.

def split_sentences(text):
    text = " ".join(text.split())
    bounds = []
    for m in re.finditer(r'[.!?]["\u201d\u2019]?\s+', text):
        before = text[:m.start()].rstrip()
        tok = before.split()[-1].lower().rstrip(".") if before.split() else ""
        if tok in ABBREV:
            continue
        bounds.append(m.end())
    out, start = [], 0
    for b in bounds:
        out.append(text[start:b].strip())
        start = b
    tail = text[start:].strip()
    if tail:
        out.append(tail)
    return [s for s in out if s]

    text = " ".join(text.split())
    bounds = []
    for m in re.finditer(r'[.!?]["\u201d\u2019]?\s+', text):
        before = text[:m.start()].rstrip()
        tok = before.split()[-1].lower().rstrip(".") if before.split() else ""
        if tok in ABBREV:
            continue
        bounds.append(m.end())
    out, start = [], 0
    for b in bounds:
        out.append(text[start:b].strip())
        start = b
    tail = text[start:].strip()
    if tail:
        out.append(tail)
    return [s for s in out if s]

He had chosen King Lear, because it was a great play, and because he had always wanted to direct it, and because he had forgotten, or had never known, that King Lear has a cast of twenty, and that our village has a population of four hundred, of whom perhaps ten can act, and of whom perhaps two are willing to admit it, in public, on a Tuesday evening, in the village hall, in front of Mr. Pemberton, who was, as everyone knew, a difficult man, to audition for, because he shouted, and because he wept, at the auditions, when the acting was bad, and the acting was always bad, and so Mr. Pemberton wept, a great deal, at auditions.\n\nOn the Tuesday evening, seven people came. and because she had a laugh, which she described as "a Regan laugh", and which she demonstrated, at the audition, and which made everyone in the room, including Mr. Pemberton, take a step backwards, which Fiona took as a compliment, and which it was, in a way.\n\nAnd there was me. Please, never laugh like that, except on stage, and preferably, not at me."\n\nAnd I played the King of France. I said my lines, all four of them, clearly, and I looked at Poppy, as Cordelia, and I said, "She is herself a dowry," which is what the King of France says, about Cordelia, and Poppy looked at me, and she smiled, a little, and Mr. Pemberton said, "You. You are the King of France. You have four lines, and you said them well, and you looked at Cordelia, as if you meant them, and that is more than most Kings of France do, in most productions, in most villages, in most times."\n\nAnd so we were cast. Mrs. Abernathy as Lear. Bert as the Fool. Sanjay as Edmund. Poppy as Cordelia. Gerald as Gloucester. Fiona as Regan. And me, as the King of France. And Mr. Pemberton, who had directed twelve plays, and who had learned nothing from any of them, looked at us, seven people, in a village hall, on a Tuesday evening, and he wept, and he said, "This. This is a cast. This is a play. This is King Lear. And we will be magnificent. Or we will be terrible. But we will be together, and we will do it, and that is what theatre is, in the end: seven people, in a village hall, who cannot act, except for one, who can, and who will carry us all, and we will be grateful, and we will try, and trying, in theatre, is everything."\n\nWe rehearsed, for three months. We learned our lines. We built a set, out of cardboard, and paint, and hope. Mrs. Abernathy wore her crown, from 1974. Bert wore his hat, with bells. Sanjay snarled. Poppy was beautiful. Gerald lost his glasses, twice a rehearsal. Fiona laughed, and everyone stepped backwards. And I, the King of France, said my four lines, and looked at Poppy, and Poppy smiled, a little, and then a little more, and then, one evening, after rehearsal, she said, "You are a good King of France," and I said, "Thank you. You are a good Cordelia," and she said, "Would you like to have tea, sometime? Not as the King of France. As yourself." And I said yes, and we had tea, and then we had tea again, and then we were not just the King of France, and Cordelia, but ourselves, and ourselves, it turned out, liked each other, very much, which was a better ending, than any in King Lear, which, as everyone knows, ends badly, for almost everyone, except the King of France, who leaves, early, with Cordelia, and who, in our production, left, early, with Cordelia, and lived happily ever after, or at least, happily, for now, which is the best any of us can hope for, in theatre, or in life, or in a village hall, on a Tuesday evening, in front of Mr. Pemberton, who wept, when he saw us, together, and who said, "That. That is acting. That is real. And that is why we do it, all of us, even when we cannot act, especially when we cannot act, because sometimes, in trying, we find something real, and something true, and something that lasts, longer than the play, and longer than the applause, and that is the audition, and the rehearsal, and the performance, all in one, and it is enough."\n\nThe rehearsals were a disaster, in the best possible way. In the first week, Mrs. Abernathy\'s crown, from 1974, broke, in the middle of the storm scene, and the cardboard fell, in pieces, onto the stage, and Mrs. Abernathy, without missing a beat, picked up a piece, and held it, like a sceptre, and said, "Blow, winds, and crack your cheeks!" and Mr. Pemberton, who had been about to weep, laughed, instead, and said, "Mrs. Abernathy, that was magnificent. Keep the broken crown. It is better broken. Lear is broken. The crown should be broken, too." In the second week, Gerald lost his glasses, on stage, during the blinding scene, which was, Mr. Pemberton said, "method acting, of the highest order, although unintentional, and although Gerald could not see, which made it, in a way, more authentic, because Gloucester, after all, cannot see either." In the third week, Bert\'s hat, with bells, lost a bell, which rolled, across the stage, during the most solemn moment in the play, and Bert, chasing it, on all fours, in the middle of a tragedy, made the entire cast laugh, and Mr. Pemberton, wiping his eyes, said, "Bert, you are the Fool. The Fool chases bells. It is in the text. Somewhere. Probably. Keep chasing the bell, Bert. It is the truest thing in this play."\n\nThe dress rehearsal was the worst, and the best. The set fell down, twice. The lights went out, once. Fiona\'s Regan laugh made a child in the audience cry, although there was no audience, only Mr. Pemberton, and the child was Mr. Pemberton\'s grandson, who had come to watch, and who cried, and Fiona apologised, and the grandson said, "It is all right. She is scary. That is good. Villains should be scary." And Poppy, as Cordelia, forgot a line, and I, as the King of France, prompted her, gently, and she remembered, and she smiled at me, and Mr. Pemberton, watching, said, "That. That is what theatre is. Not the lines, perfectly said, but the lines, remembered, together, and the smile, and the helping, and the being there, for each other, on stage, in the dark, when the set falls down, and the lights go out, and the bell rolls away, and the crown breaks, and still, we go on, because the play must go on, and because we are together, and because that is enough."\n\nOn the night of the performance, the village hall was full. Four hundred people, in a hall built for two hundred, sitting on chairs, and on the floor, and standing, at the back, and Mr. Pemberton, backstage, wept, as he always did, and said, "This is it. This is the night. Be magnificent. Or be terrible. But be together." The curtain — which was not a curtain, but a bedsheet, hung on a rope — went up, and Mrs. Abernathy, as Lear, in her broken crown, came on, and she was magnificent, loudly, and with great conviction, and the audience, which had come expecting to be polite, was silent, and then it laughed, in the right places, and it gasped, in the right places, and it cried, in the right places, and Bert, as the Fool, jingled, and joked, and the audience loved him, and Sanjay, as Edmund, snarled, and the audience hated him, which was the point, and Poppy, as Cordelia, was beautiful, and clear, and the audience held its breath, and Gerald, as Gloucester, lost his glasses, on stage, in front of four hundred people, and carried on, without them, and the audience, which knew about Gerald\'s glasses, applauded, and Fiona, as Regan, laughed, her Regan laugh, and the audience, all four hundred of them, took a step backwards, together, in their seats, which was a remarkable thing to see, and which Fiona took as the greatest compliment of her life.\n\nAnd I, the King of France, said my four lines, and I looked at Poppy, and Poppy looked at me, and the audience, which knew, by then, about the King of France, and Cordelia, and about the tea, and about ourselves, applauded, louder than for any other moment in the play, because the audience, in a village, knows when something is real, and when something is acted, and the King of France, and Cordelia, were real, and the audience knew it, and they applauded, for us, and for the play, and for Mrs. Abernathy, and Bert, and Sanjay, and Gerald, and Fiona, and Mr. Pemberton, who wept, in the wings, and who came on, at the end, for the curtain call, and who said, to the audience: "Thank you. Thank you for coming. Thank you for laughing, and for gasping, and for crying, and for stepping backwards, together, when Regan laughed. This play was a tragedy, and it was a comedy, and it was a disaster, and it was magnificent, and it was ours, and we did it, together, seven people, in a village hall, who cannot act, except for one, who can, and who carried us all, and I am proud, and I am grateful, and I will direct another play, next year, and I hope you will all audition, again, and bring your own crowns, if you have them, and your own hats, with bells, and your own Regan laughs, and we will do it again, because that is what theatre is, in a village, and in the world: people, together, trying, and failing, and trying again, and finding, in the trying, something real, and something true, and something that lasts.'
